articles.title: [OPINION] How did the Philippine government perform at COP31?
articles.summary: Any COP pavilion is worth it if it translates pledges into grants, investments, and other finance that does not burden Filipinos

blocks.text: Any COP pavilion is worth it if it translates pledges into grants, investments, and other finance that does not burden Filipinos

Unknown to millions of Filipinos preoccupied with the ASEAN Summit and the latest controversies hitting the Marcos Jr. administration, the future of the country was being shaped at a more important conference thousands of kilometers away.

At the recent 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, the Philippine government launched a set of new plans and frameworks that would redefine the direction of national climate action for at least the next decade.
At the Philippine Hub (the country’s pavilion at COP31), the government presented to the global community the following major plans:

items: The 2026 Nationally Determined Contribution, which states that the country will avoid and reduce its emissions by 75% within the next decade;
The Just Transition Framework, which charts the nation’s pathway of low-emissions, climate-resilient development where no one is left behind;
The Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework, which aims to accelerate climate change mitigation through market-based mechanisms that attract more investments; and
The Philippine Climate Finance Strategy, which outlines how the nation will secure finance from public and private sectors, here and abroad.

blocks.text: This is not to mention findings from notable studies on health, inequality, energy, climate budget, and other issues from both government and nongovernmental groups.

These are plans and frameworks many sectors — civil society, private sector, development partners, and even other government agencies — have helped shape to varying extents and have been waiting to be finalized for years.

These launches were done at the Philippine Hub to directly inform COP31 — which has at least 92,000 participants, the most in history — that the country has never been more ready to accelerate its climate solutions.

With global warming set to exceed the long-term goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius under the Paris Agreement in the near future, it is critical for the Philippines to not only show institutional readiness to implement its own solutions but also scale up its responses to protect its vulnerable communities and ecosystems.
To give credit where it’s due, compared to a few years ago, the conduct of the Philippine Hub was relatively more inclusive. There is room for improvement, but that is worth recognizing.

Nevertheless, it is also necessary to examine whether all of these new plans and frameworks are sufficient to align the Philippines with the 1.5°C goal. It is part of the nation’s equitable responsibility as part of the ruling under the International Court of Justice Advisory Opinion on climate change released in 2025. But another question is worth reflecting on.

At COP30 in Brazil in 2025, the Philippines was criticized by many, including civil society groups, for not having its own pavilion compared to its ASEAN neighbors. This year, around P23 million was set under the 2026 General Appropriations Act to ensure the country would have its own space to conduct side events, meetings, and the launching of plans and frameworks.

It is understandable to be skeptical about such expenditures, especially given the nation’s economic state, the lingering aftermath of the flood control corruption scandal, and the numerous crises it faces, including the climate one. This is also considering that COP31 failed to even produce a major agreement — the first time since 2009, coincidentally when the Philippines enacted the Climate Change Act.
Unfortunately, COP pavilions have become notoriously expensive over the years, with larger country pavilions costing about twice as much.

Yet it did not stop other vulnerable countries, especially small Pacific island nations, from securing their own pavilions. They understand the need to send powerful messages of hope and progress through their spaces and to keep the pressure on developed countries and polluters to pay up, in one way or another.
This is why context matters; on that note, it is necessary for the Philippines to have a COP pavilion. The question of whether it was worth the cost is an entirely different discussion.

Any COP pavilion is worth it if it translates pledges into grants, investments, and other finance that does not burden Filipinos. It is worth it if all the launched plans and reports in those two weeks lead to reduced emissions, vulnerabilities, and losses and damages, enhanced climate resilience, and other benefits felt on the ground.

These messages were also mentioned by three of the country’s lead negotiators: Robert Borje (co-head of delegation and overall co-facilitator on finance), Yolando Velasco (on finance), and Noralene Uy (on adaptation) during side events at the Philippine Hub.

Borje also highlighted during the closing plenary the necessity of finance in enabling implementation of solutions that developing countries like the Philippines need, although there is uncertainty as to whether the country was favoring or rejecting the adoption of the proposed cover decision text.

Every word said in side events, every named partner plastered on its walls, every commitment to be made — everything about what the Philippine government does at climate COPs must be grounded in the pursuit of climate justice for the most vulnerable.
As challenging as engaging in climate COPs is, a significant issue remains: there is some misalignment between what the government pushes for in the negotiations and what is happening back home.

This must be addressed if we don’t want another failure like the flood control corruption scandal to happen again. Polluters must pay, including those who hinder renewable energy development because they don’t think it’s profitable. Communities must be supported to claim their space in decision-making spaces and demand finance and other means of implementation to address climate impacts.

The work at COP31 is over. The Philippines has shown its cards at the world’s biggest stage. Now the next year of climate action begins. We’ll see whether words will be turned into action. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Wildfire victim trying to buy new Flin Flon, Man., home loses $170K in lawyer impersonation scam
articles.summary: Five Manitobans in the last two months have fallen victim to a fraud scheme where scammers infiltrate lawyers' emails and redirect money. One woman in Flin Flon, trying to buy a new home after losing…

image.caption: Lisa Holmes sits in her parents' home in Flin Flon, Man., where she's lived since her home in nearby Denare Beach, Sask., was destroyed in a 2025 fire. She tried to buy a home of her own in Flin Flon earlier this year, but fell victim to an online scam and lost over $170,000. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

Five Manitobans in the last two months have fallen victim to a fraud scheme where scammers infiltrate lawyers' emails and redirect money. One woman in Flin Flon, trying to buy a new home after losing hers in a wildfire, is out more than $170,000.
Nearly $1M lost in 5 cases in recent months targeting lawyers and clients: Law Society of Manitoba

A Flin Flon woman whose home was destroyed in a wildfire has lost tens of thousands of dollars after falling prey to an online impersonation scam — one that has cost Manitobans nearly $1 million in just two months.

She was one of several people targeted recently by what the Manitoba Law Society calls a "payment misdirection fraud," where a scammer pretends to be a person's lawyer, orchestrates a large payment, then takes the money, often leaving the victim with little recourse to recover it.

Lisa Holmes was living in the northeastern Saskatchewan community of Denare Beach, about 20 kilometres southwest of Flin Flon, when a forest fire hit the area in June 2025. Her home and possessions were destroyed.
Holmes had limited insurance coverage and couldn't fully rebuild, so she moved in with her parents while trying to buy a new house.
The remains of Lisa Holmes's house in Denare Beach, Sask., which was destroyed by a wildfire on June 2, 2025. (Submitted by Lisa Holmes)

She found one for sale in Flin Flon and began working with a lawyer, Dayna Zaharia in The Pas, Man., to buy it. They communicated through email and used the online Docusign service for contract signatures, Holmes said.

She was instructed to send a wire transfer for more than $170,000 to a bank account, where it would be held until the sale was finalized, and sent that transfer through Flin Flon's RBC branch on Oct. 5, she said.
But she wasn't messaging Zaharia about that transfer — it was a scammer impersonating the lawyer.

"I didn't find out until a few days into it that the email was hacked," said Holmes. "Someone was impersonating myself and my lawyer and they were sending emails to one another, but we didn't know … until after we talked."
By then, the money was gone. Holmes didn't get the house. She's still living with her parents and worried she'll never get her money back.
"I was so excited that I was going to get my home. I never thought I was going to be blindsided like that."
Bank says client responsible
Holmes said she and Zaharia contacted the Law Society of Manitoba, which says they were targeted in a growing wave of payment misdirection fraud.
Zaharia declined an interview request, citing attorney-client privilege. Law society representatives also declined, saying they do not publicly comment on individual cases.
The regulatory body issued a statement Nov. 18, saying it's aware of five cases of "payment misdirection" fraud in Manitoba in the past two months alone, with almost $1 million lost.

The law society said scammers use the "infiltrated" accounts of lawyers or employees to send an email to another lawyer's client, a financial institution or a third party, telling them to send funds to a bank account that's actually controlled by the fraudster.

In most of the recent cases, it appears there was no insurance, the statement said. The scams went beyond real estate transactions, and two cases involved law firms that don't even have trust accounts.
RBC says as scams become more sophisticated, people should independently verify banking information before sending money. (David Donnelly/CBC)
Holmes notified RBC Nov. 4, filing a complaint stating it failed to protect her from financial abuse.
In an email response Holmes shared with CBC, the bank maintained she is "held responsible due to participation in fraud or scam," and said it considers the matter closed.
In a statement to CBC, an RBC spokesperson said as scams become more sophisticated, people should independently verify banking information before sending money.

items: Winnipeg woman slams bank's decision not to refund her after 'dumbfounding' scam

blocks.text: The bank said it provides information about fraud prevention on its website, as does the Canadian Anti-Scam Coalition, which RBC is part of.
"You wonder, how does this happen? How does someone just steal over $170,000 and there's no accountability?" said Holmes.
"It would be so simple for the bank to just do a second check, right?"
Preventative steps
Holmes contacted the RCMP, who said they are investigating hers and similar cases.
Cpl. Ricky Perkins, who works with the Manitoba RCMP's cyber and financial crime unit, says they often see scams begin with clicking a link in a phishing email.
Scammers will "infiltrate the system" and set up rules in email programs like Outlook or Gmail, he said.
"Then they'll monitor the activity to see kind of who's who in the zoo … [and] take over the account."
Cpl. Ricky Perkins works with Manitoba RCMP's cyber and financial crime unit. He says scams like these are becoming more frequent and more sophisticated. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)
He said there are email precautions people can take to avoid being hacked, including checking sent and trash folders for any sent emails that don't look familiar.
"That would be a really good indicator that the account's been breached," he said.

The law society also advises lawyers to check their email folders for suspicious activity. It also says they should tell clients they won't accept or change payment instructions by email, and should confirm any payment information by phone.

items: Same scam. 2 countries. Why Canadians don’t get their money back

blocks.text: If people are targeted in a scam, they can try to cancel or reverse the payment through their bank or contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, said Cpl. Perkins.
"Every case is different. In some cases we have recovered funds. In other cases, unfortunately, we can't," he said.

"There have been instances where people have been charged, and then obviously there's cases where the funds do end up in kind of the multiverse, so to speak. It's a difficult path for us to continue to follow."

Holmes holds one of the few things left after her Denare Beach home burned down in 2025 — a school art project she made as a child, with her handprint pressed onto plaster. She hopes RCMP will catch the person who scammed her. (Eric Westhaver/CBC)
RCMP said no arrests have been made in Holmes's case.
She said she hopes she'll recover her money and buy a new home, but if the bank and insurance can't help, she hopes the Mounties get their culprit — and that person will pay.
"[The courts] can tell them to pay it back if they have the money, but they also tell me that could take years," she said.
"I have a little bit of hope, but I don't have a lot of hope."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Westhaver is a journalist with CBC Manitoba, working out of Flin Flon. Born and raised in the north, Eric worked with the Flin Flon Reminder for nine years before joining CBC in 2025. His email is eric.westhaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Health Canada seizes peptides from Toronto shop, warns of health risks of unregulated market
articles.summary: Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides.

blocks.text: Toronto·New
Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides.
Experts warn products being sold are unregulated and untested
Why Health Canada seized 'unauthorized injectable peptides' from Toronto shop
Health Canada has seized a number of injectable peptides from a store in Toronto's Queen West neighbourhood, CBC News has learned.

Health Canada confirmed it confiscated and is now testing a number of what it called "unauthorized injectable peptides" from the shop, Not Peptides, on Nov. 9. It also seized bacteriostatic water products, which are often used to reconstitute freeze-dried peptides.

The federal health agency has warned the Canadian public against using unauthorized peptides, which many have purchased online or acquired through compounding pharmacies. The agency said it wasn't able to provide any further detail about its ongoing investigation at Not Peptides, which runs both a bricks-and-mortar and online shop.
"Selling unauthorized health products is illegal," Geneviève Lapierre, a spokesperson for the department, said in an emailed statement.
"Health Canada will continue to seize unauthorized peptide products and disrupt distribution channels to remove these products from the Canadian market."
Not Peptides, which remained open after the seizure, did not respond to CBC Toronto's request for comment.

Peptides are short chains of linked amino acids that serve as the building blocks of proteins, and occur naturally in the body. But the injectable peptides being sold by Not Peptides are largely unproven products that, in many cases, have become popular as fitness influencers claim they can fuel muscle recovery and reverse the signs of aging.

One vial for sale at Not Peptides, a mix of three different peptides including BPC-157, is described on the store's website as being "engineered for synergistic skin renewal, connective-tissue integrity, and accelerated wound closure."
Experts have highlighted there are no large-scale human efficacy trials for BPC-157.

items: Doctors are using a regulatory gap to prescribe an unauthorized peptide

blocks.text: What's behind the peptide boom?
Some peptide-based medications have legitimate medical applications and have been approved for use in Canada.

Experts like David Sabatino, a professor in the Department of Chemistry at Carleton University, have pointed out they can be used properly, highlighting the popularity of peptide-based medications like GLP-1 — often better known under brand names like Ozempic.
But that's fueled interest in other untested peptides, which come with more risk.
“We should take extra caution and be very careful with the risks that are associated with using peptides that have not gone through that approval process,” Sabatino said.

One of his biggest concerns is the potential for contamination in products that have not undergone proper quality control. Sabatino pointed to reports of contaminants, toxins and bacteria in unregulated products, which can lead to infections and other serious complications.

items: Are you a Torontonian who uses unregulated peptides? Email us at TOnews@cbc.ca because we'd like to hear from you for future stories on this topic.

blocks.text: Health Canada warns on its website that taking untested peptides increases the risk of hormonal imbalance, mood swings, blood sugar imbalance, liver or kidney damage, blood clots and even the growth of cancerous tumours.

Public Health Ontario told CBC News it does not systematically collect specific emergency department visit data related to peptide use, making it difficult to determine how many people may be experiencing complications.
City not taking enforcement action against shop
The situation has echoes of Toronto’s early cannabis dispensary crackdown, when stores continued reopening despite repeated police raids. Several of those shops are still operating in Toronto.
The City of Toronto said Not Peptides doesn't have a business licence because of the type of service it provides.
"As a result, no city business licence is required and no licensing enforcement action has been taken," spokesperson Mahreen Dasoo said in an email.
How Canadians are getting unauthorized peptides
Toronto police said in an email its officers weren't involved in Health Canada's seizure.

Health Canada has made similar seizures before, including a wellness shop in Ottawa. Three days before Not Peptides was investigated, Health Canada also issued a public warning after lab testing found bacteria in some peptide products sold by two online retailers.
"Do not buy or use these products," the warning states.
'My first concern if public safety,' physician says
The popularity of peptides, particularly among people seeking cosmetic and performance-related benefits, is growing according to Dr. Jennifer Pearlman.
The Toronto physician who administers peptide therapies says social media influencers have also played a role in promoting these products.
Peptides have already been used in cosmetic products for decades, she says.
When administered safely, and under the supervision of a physician, Pearlman says there are benefits and peptides in the world of medicine hold great promise.
Dr. Jennifer Pearlman is the medical director and CEO of Pearl Rejuvenation in Toronto's Yonge-St. Clair neighbourhood. (Submitted by Jennifer Pearlman)
"They hold enormous therapeutic potential but they are biologically active compounds," she said, adding she was alarmed by what she saw on the shop's website.
"My first concern is public safety. Like all medicines, peptides should be prescribed by a physician to a patient, carefully considering both risk and benefit."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Talia Ricci is a TV, radio and web reporter at CBC Toronto. She enjoys covering offbeat human interest stories and exposing social justice issues. Talia has also reported in London, Ont. and Winnipeg, Man. You can email story ideas to talia.ricci@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI lets you buy flowers for your girlfriend. Some streamers say it's too woke
articles.summary: The new Grand Theft Auto VI brings old classics back to the franchise, but this iteration also has some changes. Instead of hiring sex workers, the early part of the game has you doing chores for…

image.caption: Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, pictured here, are the main characters of the new Grand Theft Auto VI. But some streamers aren't happy with some of the early missions that give you the option to do some chores to improve the characters' relationship. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The new Grand Theft Auto VI brings old classics back to the franchise, but this iteration also has some changes. Instead of hiring sex workers, the early part of the game has you doing chores for your in-game girlfriend, like buying her flowers and fixing the leak in the roof.
Despite pushback, the game has still made billions in sales since its release
The new Grand Theft Auto VI brings old classics back to the franchise: stealing cars, flying planes, evading cops. But this iteration also has some changes.

Instead of hiring sex workers, the early part of the game has you doing chores for your in-game girlfriend, like buying her flowers and fixing the leak in the roof. And as a result, a fringe group of players and streamers say the latest version of Grand Theft Auto is too woke.

"The game is presenting this option of treating women respectfully," said Joshua Foust, an assistant professor in public relations at Syracuse University, who studies the intersection of gaming and gender.

"And the response, at least from these accounts that seem to be mad about it, is that even the request to treat a woman respectfully in a game, they find offensive and somehow diminishing of their own sense of manhood."
That's apparently not what Braden Eric Peters, better known as the looksmaxxing influencer Clavicular, signed up for.
"GTA 6 is insanely cucked, half of the missions are jestermaxing and simping for girls," Peters, who is currently on trial for rape, posted on X.
Despite pushback, the game recorded $3.79 billion US in retail sales in the first 24 hours of ‌its launch. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images)

Despite this pushback, the open-world action adventure game isn't struggling to sell. The game ‌recorded $3.79 billion US in retail sales in the first 24 ⁠hours ⁠of ‌its launch, according to game developer Rockstar Games, making it the world's biggest video game release ever.

"If you look at something like Grand Theft Auto, that is a prime example of how the online feedback from certain groups of people in no way mirrors what's actually going on here," said Alyssa Mercante, a culture critic and gaming journalist.
Buying flowers and putting up drywall
The game lets you play as both Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, though you spend a majority of the early missions controlling Jason.

During that time — amid smuggling drugs and stealing cars — players have the option to perform what is essentially a "honey-do" list, including putting up drywall, painting the bedroom and fixing the stairs leading up to your house.
You can even go buy Lucia flowers (she is just getting out of a prison, after all), though all of these tasks are optional.
Early in the game, players are given the option to do some work on Jason's house, pictured here, to improve the relationship between Jason and Lucia. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)
In another part of the early game, you have to unclog a woman's sink for her, which did not impress streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold.
"Are you kidding me?" he said while streaming. "Why can't she do this? Why do I have to do this for her?"

Foust says that underneath what he calls this "toxic criticism" is a belief by some that these games should only be made for them and shouldn't serve anyone else. He says this is especially true among streamers who play these games professionally and expect everything in these games to be specifically tailored to them.
"That's not me diagnosing anything, just like, usually, if you're unable to accept that some things are not for you, that's emotionally immature," said Foust.
Monetized rage bait?
Mercante, who is currently working on a book about rage baiting, says all of that pushback may not be totally genuine.

These streamers — such as Hoyt, who has millions of subscribers on his video channels — make their money off people watching their tirades. And clips posted on platforms such as X are often boosted by the algorithm, she says.
"Money is a hell of a drug," said Mercante.
She says many of these streamers who make money of this behaviour either end up believing the things they spout on their streams or adopting it as their online persona.
What makes the release of Grand Theft Auto VI so special?
She says many of the people who follow streamers like Hoyt may watch the clips, and may even share them, but often are still buying the game.
And she says Grand Theft Auto VI isn't an albatross — most major video game releases over the past few years have come under fire by this same group for things it considers woke.

When Assassin's Creed Shadows came out in 2025, some people complained about it featuring a Black lead character. Also last year, the Ghost of Tsushima sequel — Ghost of Yōtei — received some backlash for featuring a female character as its protagonist.

"Of course this was going to happen with GTA. Someone is going to try and find something to trot out as an example of, you know, the 'wokeification' of video games or about how games are being taken away from straight white men," said Mercante.
The game puts a lot of focus on Jason and Lucia, pictured here, and their relationships. And some streamers aren't happy about it. (Rockstar Games/Take-Two Interactive)

Overall, Mercante says studios aren't too concerned with this type of reaction. While an online movement may impact small independent studios, she says large publishers like Take-Two Interactive, which publishes Grand Theft Auto VI, aren't going to see this pushback affect their bottom line.

So, what do you do if you see a particularly outrageous review? Mercante says to take a look at who is posting it, and who stands to gain from it. If someone has a verification checkmark on X, they are paying to be able to monetize their posts.
"Recognize that, in many cases, this type of content is meant to manipulate and is meant to misinform and ultimately is meant to put money in the pocket of the person posting it," she said.
"We live in a place where people don't trust the media anymore, but I promise you a content creator who is monetizing their — for lack of a better term — shit posts, is not more trustworthy."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Philip Drost is a network senior writer for CBC News based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 'Brexit means Brexit' no more? Why the U.K. now wants closer ties with the EU
articles.summary: Brexit might not have meant Brexit after all. At least, the door to a "Breturn," as they’re already calling it here, has been nudged open a crack or two by Britain’s Labour Prime Minister Andy…

image.caption: From left to right, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa grasp hands in a gesture of solidary after an EU-U.K. Summit on Nov. 20 in Brussels. Ten years after Brexit, Burnham looks to be pushing for closer

blocks.text: Remember that old slogan, "Brexit means Brexit," in the wake of Britain’s decision to leave the European Union after the 2016 referendum pitted leavers against remainers?

It was relentlessly repeated by former British prime minister Theresa May — herself a remainer — as she sought to convince her own governing Conservatives that she wouldn’t allow any backsliding on the decision while negotiating the terms of Britain’s exit from the EU.

Well, it turns out Brexit might not have meant Brexit after all. At least, the door to a "Breturn," as they’re already calling it here, has been nudged open a crack or two by Britain’s Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
He’s been flying a few trial balloons.

"In the decade since Brexit, our standing in the world has diminished," he told a black-tie event at Guildhall in the city of London last week, just days before an EU-U.K. Summit heralded a deal to reduce some red tape on exports and improve student mobility in both directions.
"We treated both allies and institutions with insufficient care."
Perhaps one reason he’s becoming bolder on the issue is because opinion polls are on his side.
Fifty-eight percent of Britons now think leaving the EU was a mistake, according to a recent YouGov poll that surveyed 2,019 people.

"The majority of Brits realized that they were lied to by various politicians … and they have actually woken up to the fact that they’re not better off," said Chris Riddell, a political cartoonist for the Observer newspaper who would like to see the U.K. rejoin the EU.
"I’ve been drawing a Brexit ogre for the last decade. I’m looking forward to drawing maybe a tombstone and he’s been laid to rest, finally."
One of political cartoonist Chris Riddell's depictions of the Brexit ogre. (Chris Riddell)
Among the most toxic debates in recent U.K. history
Still, Burnham is treading carefully, talking about resetting relations before any moves toward rejoining, insisting he’ll never move ahead of British public opinion.

The Brexit debate was perhaps one of the most toxic in recent British history, with 51.9 per cent voting to leave and 48.1 per cent voting to stay. Many of those in favour of leaving argued that Brussels had too much influence over U.K. decision-making, especially on the control of its borders.
Since leaving the EU, the U.K.'s GDP per capita is now six to eight per cent lower than it would have been had the country remained, by one estimate.
In the wake of the EU-U.K. summit, all five of the Conservative prime ministers from the 2016 referendum on have risen like ghosts of Christmases past to warn Burnham against reopening the debate.

David Cameron, who campaigned to remain after calling the referendum and then resigned after the result, told Bloomburg that Britain’s poor economic growth was not, as Burnham argued, because of Brexit.
Bre-turn? Reset talks spark debate over Britain rejoining the EU
And Theresa May, of "Brexit means Brexit" fame, told the BBC that she was "aghast" at the talk of rejoining, saying Burnham needed to "move on."

May was eventually felled by divisions within her Conservative Party over how "hard" Britain’s exit from the EU should be and replaced by Boris Johnson, who recently told the Daily Telegraph that Britain would still back Brexit today.
Liz Truss, who became the shortest-serving prime minister in U.K. history after replacing Johnson, said the idea of Britain "reshackling" itself to the EU was "sheer lunacy."

items: Canada's new relationship with EU will be 'closer to membership' than ever, senior officials say
Brexit, 10 years later: What a regret-fuelled British town can teach Canada about referendums

blocks.text: Her successor, Rishi Sunak, said it would be a "huge distraction."
It could well be a cautionary tale for Burnham, given the role that Brexit played in much of the Conservative Party’s infighting. But he said on Monday that he wouldn't be listening to them.
"They left Britain with a bad Brexit deal that has hit growth over the past decade," he told British media. "They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did."
Pro-Brexit supporters attend the Brexit Day Celebration Party hosted by Leave Means Leave at Parliament Square in January 2020 in London. (Jeff J. Mitchell/Getty Images)
Economist Patrick Minford, who campaigned for Brexit, argues Britain’s sluggish economy isn’t suffering from leaving the EU, but from bad management.
"The EU would have enormous power over us, through its ability to regulate all aspects of our lives," he told CBC News. "And that was the central non-economic issue in the debate."
New decade, new world
But Burnham and other supporters of rejoining the EU argue that the world has changed over the past 10 years — and with it, attitudes toward the European Union.
Labour MP and former U.K. foreign secretary David Lammy puts part of that shift down to the Trump factor.
"Just like Canada is reeling from a different relationship with the United States, so Europe is reeling from a different relationship to the United States," he said.
"Sovereignty disappears very quickly in the current geopolitical environment, unless you are in concert with other shared friends."
He’s not surprised that Canada has been exploring closer ties with the European Union.
Canada deepens ties with Europe at summit in Ireland
"The space between us is so slim we’re better huddled together in the best formation," he said.
"That does not, of course, mean that we do not have the closest of relationships with our friends in the United States."
Reopening old wounds
Even some Britons who voted to remain in the EU worry about the possibility of reopening old wounds.
"So there’s an aspect where you just say, 'Well, hold on a minute. If people have voted, you do have to respect it,'" said Bleue Granada, a retired woman.
"But at the same time, I think we need a much more intelligent debate, more informed debate. And I think that was lacking and I think people are a lot wiser now."
Bleue Granada, a retired woman in the U.K., says the country needs a more informed debate on the issue of Brexit. (Katie Pedersen/CBC)
David Arvidsson, a dual Swedish and British citizen, was studying in England when the U.K. voted to leave the EU.
"[As a] student in Cambridge, you had basically not met a single person in favour of Brexit, so it came as a shock," he said.
"[Pushing to rejoin] will lead to a lot of arguments," he said. "I do think that a majority would be in favour of it. I do feel that we lost something in the U.K. when we left the EU."
Kenneth Robbie, another resident, says he decided how to vote on his way to the polls during the last referendum, eventually casting his ballot to remain.
"I just hope that if it’s going to become a live, red-hot issue again, that we can discuss it calmly and avoid another referendum, because the referendum 10 years ago, I think, was very divisive."
'Unthinkable' to rejoin without referendum
But when pressed on the questions of a referendum in Parliament on Monday, Burnham replied that it would be "unthinkable" for any British prime minister to rejoin the EU without one.
David Lammy, the Labour MP, agrees. He wants his party to fight the next election with a commitment to rejoin the EU.
Brexit continues to be controversial, with this protest in September 2023 showing a man holding an anti-Brexit sign, in central London. (Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images)
"We will then have a negotiation. We will have a referendum. And the deal will be done by the election after the next one."

items: Why is it so much easier to ditch a prime minister in the U.K. than in Canada?

blocks.text: But it is a gamble.
The Brexit genie has never really stayed in the bottle, managing to bedevil British politics before, during and after the referendum.

articles.title: Teodoro says businesses should strengthen supply chain resilience amid China concerns
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Tuesday said businesses in the Philippines should strengthen their supply chain resilience following concerns with their existing trade ties with China amid…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 4:58pm

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. on Tuesday said businesses in the Philippines should strengthen their supply chain resilience following concerns with their existing trade ties with China amid the tension in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).

At a press conference, Teodoro was asked about reports that some businesses were concerned that the Philippines' firm stance on the WPS could affect imports, exports and supply chains involving China.
“It behooves businesses, particularly those who perform a function which is vested with public interest, a critical service to make their supply chains more resilient,” he said.
Teodoro cited the COVID-19 pandemic as an example of the importance of preparing for supply chain disruptions.

“The pandemic proved that if you don't invest in the technology, you'll be at the last of the line when the vaccines came out. So, I think, I understand that businesses have comfortable supply chains with China, but it is a responsible thing to be resilient,” he added.
Asked whether business leaders had raised concerns with him about his position on China, Teodoro said none had directly approached him.
“Now, if the businesses feel one way or the other towards me, then they can tell me or they can announce it if they want to. I don't mind,” Teodoro said.

Earlier, several business and civil society groups have called on Philippine and Chinese officials to exercise sobriety and restraint and renew diplomatic engagement amid recent heated public exchanges between government officials and the Chinese Embassy.
In a joint statement, the groups warned against the dangers of public recriminations and inflammatory rhetoric, urging both sides to return to established diplomatic channels. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Social media companies could be fined 5% of global revenue after Labor and Greens join forces on online safety laws
articles.summary: Individual Australians will be able to sue big tech firms for harm suffered online under compromise deal

blocks.text: Big tech companies may face “multibillion-dollar” fines and individuals could sue social media companies in court under Australia’s new digital duty of care laws, with the Greens to support the bill’s passage after extracting major amendments from Labor.
From late 2027, Australians will also be able opt out of addictive online algorithms under the new legislation, while the “endless scroll” of social media feeds may also cease.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, confirmed that, in extreme breaches, social media and tech companies could face fines of up to 5% of their global revenue if they flout the new laws. She said she had already met with the US ambassador, David Brat, to discuss the laws, and had stared down potential legal challenges from some of the world’s most powerful firms.
“I was at the high court a couple of weeks ago as the second respondent in the case against the social media minimum age. If people want to have another go, bring it on,” Wells said on Tuesday.

The government’s legislation will pass parliament this week, potentially as soon as Tuesday afternoon, after the Greens agreed to support the bill after intense negotiations. The Coalition had opposed the laws from the outset, citing free speech and censorship concerns, leaving the Greens to negotiate with Labor.

The planned framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. Labor said it would place “an overarching obligation” on tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians” and replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content. Wells had suggested content promoting misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured by the laws.

Following discussions with the Greens, Wells on Tuesday confirmed amendments to the bill would see Australians given a “private right of action” – a local equivalent to successful laws in the US allowing citizens to sue large companies.
The government will consider setting up an independent ombudsman or watchdog for big tech, and the maximum fines for breaches of rules could reach $109m, or up to 5% of global revenue.

The Coalition will not support the bill, which is expected to be voted on in the Senate on Tuesday night. The shadow minister for industry, Andrew Hastie, claimed the duty of care would lead to “a massive imposition on free speech and political communication”.
“Whilst the government is dressing this in the language of protecting children, they’re actually moving towards censorship here, which is our main issue here,” he told the ABC.

“It vests huge amounts of power in the minister of communications and the eSafety commissioner, who basically will regulate very vaguely defined definitions of online harm. We think that’s contrary to free speech. We’d rather have debate – and this puts our country and our culture of debate at risk.”
Labor’s legislation could also draw the ire of US-based tech giants and the Trump administration.

Wells has previously said Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform would be subject to the laws but that the government had committed to “constructive dialogue” with the US, including during her Tuesday meeting with Brat.
“I think we would say there are points of differences, and we’re ironing them out,” she said.
after newsletter promotion

Meta, Google and TikTok were contacted for comment. The Tech Council of Australia, an industry body which counts Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn, OpenAI and Pinterest among its members, said it supported the legislation, but voiced concern about the amendments.

“A private right of action is a complex undertaking with significant consequences. How this is implemented is critical, and we need proper consultation to ensure that businesses are not hindered from investing in Australia. If we get this wrong, it will be counterproductive to encouraging innovation in Australia,” a spokesperson said.

Other major changes to the bill include adding “addictive” features to the list of risks that tech platforms must address, and clarifying the definitions of “hostile attitudes to women and gender equality”. Wells said this was “not about disagreeing with feminism or expressing an opinion”, but would force tech platforms to avoid exposing children to content promoting hatred of women, including violence, death threats, coercion or harassment.
She has previously stated “manosphere podcasts” would not be affected.
Amendments to the bill will also expand eSafety Commissioner powers to remove “nudify” apps and content, and stronger privacy protections.
“The Greens have long campaigned for big tech to be held accountable for the harm they profit off online,” the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said on Tuesday.

The party had long pressed for stronger fines, an ombudsman scheme and stronger action on addictive design features. Hanson-Young said that provision would have the effect of “dumping the doomscroll with rules that force tech companies to prevent harm from their addictive design feature”.
This would go alongside original requirements for social media platforms to offer an “opt-out” feature for its algorithm and suggested content.

Wells said those elements would come into force 12 months after the laws passed. She nominated design features such as “the toxic popularity meters, the endless scroll” as those which could be banned under the addictive features stipulation, but said final decisions would be made by eSafety.
The Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman, which has volunteered to act as a big tech watchdog, welcomed the move to set up an independent complaints mechanism.
“Online services are a core part of our lives. It’s great that Australians will soon have access to a free, fair and independent dispute resolution scheme when big tech gets things wrong.”

articles.title: Asia-Pacific markets rally as Huang’s return to Nvidia reignites AI trade, despite US political backlash – business live
articles.summary: Republicans and Democrats object over Trump’s role in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO, following an affair with an alleged Chinese spy

blocks.text: Introduction: Asia-Pacific markets rally on Huang's return, despite backlash
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Jensen Huang’s surprising, and controversial, return to run Nvidia has sparked a strong rally in Asia-Pacific stock markets today,
Stocks have surged in Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and Australia, as the AI trade lurches back into life.
The Taiwanese TW50 index has surged by 9.5%, away from the seven-month high touched yesterday. In Seoul, the Kospi index has jumped by 6.5%, led by chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.
Tokyo’s Nikkei gained almost 4%, and Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 has risen by 1.8%.
That followed a surge on Wall Street last night, where Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% – adding around $950bn to the company’s value as Huang returned to the company’s HQ.

blocks.caption: Jensen Huang gestures as employees applaud his return to office after NVIDIA reinstated him as the company’s CEO, in Santa Clara, California, US November 23, 2026, in this picture obtained from social media. Photograph: NVIDIA/X/Reuters

blocks.text: Huang’s return “removes an important source of uncertainty,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo in Singapore, adding:
double quotation mark“His return restores strategic continuity at Nvidia and reduces the immediate risk of disruptions to its supply chain and technology roadmap.”

But while Wall Street recorded its best day since April 2025 (when Donald Trump paused his Liberation Day tariffs), doubts over the high valuations of AI companies, and questions over whether the industry will generate revenues to sustain their high spending on data centres, remain.
As does the political backlash against Huang’s return, and the role played by Donald Trump’s White House in pressing Nvidia to take its former CEO back.

Democrat senator Elizabeth Warren has called Huang’s restoration “reckless,” and warned that the banking committee she will head next year will be digging into whether Nvidia has complied with export controls.
She also said the Trump administration “needs to explain to Congress what ‘input’ was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement.”

Republican lawmakers also roundly criticized the Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate its chief executive, Jensen Huang, even after Donald Trump said he spoke “directly and indirectly” with board members and “convinced them” to bring him back.
Pete Ricketts, a US senator from Nebraska, wrote on X that Huang’s “behavior does not support reinstatement”, a reminder of his alleged affair with a Chinese spy.
The agenda

items: 9am GMT: IFO survey of German business confidence
11am GMT: CBI Distributive Trades survey of UK retail
2pm GMT: US house price data

blocks.text: Key events

items: 14m agoIs AI too big to fail?
30m agoHow Trump lobbied for Huang's return
49m agoLondon stock market dips in early trading
1h agoVideo: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia yesterday
2h agoUS adds Megaspeed, AI firm at center of Nvidia scandal, to trade blacklist
2h agoNvidia rejoices at Jensen Huang’s second coming
2h agoIntroduction: Asia-Pacific markets rally on Huang's return, despite backlash

blocks.text: Is AI too big to fail?
Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’.
That phrase was on everyone’s lips almost 20 years ago when the Global Financial Crisis struck, and several major banks were bailed out.
Roger Lee, head of equity strategy at investment bank Cavendish, explains:

double quotation markGiven Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the GFC, are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired? Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally.
How Trump lobbied for Huang's return
Yohannes Lowe
A day before Nvidia announced Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as its CEO, the US president, Donald Trump, dialed into the AI giant’s Sunday board meeting to argue for his return, Semafor reports.

According to the NY Times, over the weekend, Trump also asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to work with the board to assure them that Huang, who was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy, was not a national security risk.

By Monday morning, Nvidia announced Huang’s return despite its chair previously stating they did not intend to reinstate him because his personal behaviour was inconsistent with the company’s “code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”.

Reflecting a wave of anger among lawmakers at the decision, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, Robert Garcia, said in a statement on Monday that Trump’s “direct involvement” in the matter raised “serious national security and corruption questions”:

double quotation mark“We must investigate these actions. No president who has invested in a private company should be involved in their board decisions. Congress must come together in swift bipartisan action and demand answers immediately.”

Trump’s holdings of Nvidia stock rose in value by as much as $15m (£11.5m) on Monday as the share price surged after news of Huang’s reinstatement broke, the FT notes. The US president owns between $11m (£8.4m) and $55m (£42.1m) in Nvidia stock, according to a Reuters review of his 2025 annual financial disclosure and 2026 share trading disclosures.
Chinese state media have warned that Jensen Huang’s reinstatement won’t end tensions between Beijing and Washington, or restrictions on AI chip exports.
China’s Global Times newspaper published a commentary urging China to “remain vigilant” today, saying:
double quotation mark“It is foreseeable that the malicious attempts to sow discord in China-US relations will not automatically disappear simply because Huang has been reinstated.”
The article also predicted a new round of “witch hunts” could include investigation letters, delays in export licenses and congressional hearings, Bloomberg reports.
London stock market dips in early trading
London’s stock market has opened, with more of a whimper than a bang.
The FTSE 100 share index has dipped by 5 points, or 0.05%, to 10,475 points.

Why no Jensen bounce? Because European markets rallied yesterday when Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced, lifting tech companies across the continent. That pushed the FTSE 100 up by 1.3% on Monday.
Plus, as Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, explains, his return won’t ease the broader risks facing AI:

double quotation markThere’s the massive spending needed to build AI infrastructure, the pressure on free cash flow at hyperscalers — Nvidia’s biggest clients — and the need for these companies to raise money through equity or bond issuance. Then there are rising borrowing costs as inflation stays elevated and credit spreads widen, and of course the political hurdles with Democrats set to take control of Congress.
Video: Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia yesterday

blocks.caption: A display showing Asian stock markets in Taipei on November 24, 2026. Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The surge in stock markets since Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia was announced shows that investors are “willing to re-engage with the AI theme when uncertainty recedes”, says Christian Stocker, lead equity strategist for UniCredit Munich.

But… Stocker argues that the rally reflected relief that the AI supply chain and investment cycle are unlikely to be abruptly disrupted, rather than renewed conviction that all concerns have disappeared.
He told clients this morning:

double quotation markQuestions about financing structures, profitability and the ultimate returns on AI spending remain largely unresolved. In other words, the debate has shifted. Investors are no longer asking whether AI investment will continue. They are increasingly asking whether the path from investment to monetisation will be slower, more uneven and more dependent on favourable financing conditions than previously assumed. Recent market volatility suggests that the AI narrative remains intact, but the market is becoming less willing to assume a straight-line path to future earnings growth.
Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s CEO could, perhaps surprisingly, be painful for US borrowers.
That’s because America’s central bank is more likely to raise interest rates if they’re not facing a bursting AI bubble.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank explains:

double quotation markWith fears of an AI slowdown receding, it also led markets to price back in a more hawkish path for the Federal Reserve over the months ahead. So for the next meeting in December, markets are once again fully pricing in a 25bp hike, with 26.1bps priced in for that decision (+3.1bps on the day). Then looking further out, 70bps of hikes are now priced in by the September 2027 meeting, up +6.6bps relative to Friday
US adds Megaspeed, AI firm at center of Nvidia scandal, to trade blacklist
In another significant development in the Nvidia story, Megaspeed International has been placed on a US trade blacklist that bars it from buying advanced AI chips.
In a filing on Monday, the Commerce Department moved to formally add the company to its entity list. This means Megaspeed will now need approval from the commerce department to obtain US exports.
This move revelations that Jensen Huang had a ⁠relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing – a claim China has said is “groundless”.
Nvidia rejoices at Jensen Huang’s second coming
Dara Kerr
Jensen Huang made his return to Nvidia’s headquarters with a hero’s welcome yesterday.

Hours earlier he’d been reinstated as the CEO of the world’s most valuable chip company, following a whiplash series of events that involved a romantic affair with a suspected Chinese spy, a drastic plummet in the stock market, and an intervention from Donald Trump.
As Huang entered the company’s Silicon Valley office, wearing his signature dark-colored uniform, crowds of employees rushed to greet him clapping, hollering and chanting: “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!”
“I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang told employees, according to several verified videos posted to social media. The crowd went wild – it was Huang’s second coming.

articles.title: Supreme Court dismisses petitions vs Rodrigo Duterte’s ICC arrest
articles.summary: 'The Philippine courts cannot enforce the writ since he is already in the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, the Netherlands,' the High Court says

blocks.text: HIGHEST COURT. File photo of the Supreme Court of the Philippines.
Mark Z. Saludes
'The Philippine courts cannot enforce the writ since he is already in the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, the Netherlands,' the High Court says
MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court (SC), via a majority, dismissed the consolidated petitions questioning the arrest of former president Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025.
This comes days before Duterte’s International Criminal Court (ICC) trial scheduled on November 30.
In a decision penned by Associate Justice Japar Dimaampao released on Tuesday, November 24, the SC said the habeas corpus petitions were already moot or invalid.
“The Philippine courts cannot enforce the writ since he is already in the custody of the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, the Netherlands,” the High Court said.
Nine justices voted to deny the petitions, four dissented, while Associate Justice Samuel Gaerlan was on official business.

The High Court explained that a writ of habeas corpus — an extraordinary legal remedy used against illegal detention — is enforceable only within the Philippines. Duterte has been detained in The Hague since March 2025.

“This reflects the principle that a court cannot exercise authority outside its territory over persons or property located in another State,” the SC said. “Since Duterte is now under ICC custody in The Hague, Philippine courts cannot enforce a writ affecting his detention or release.”
The High Court noted that Duterte “is already participating in ICC proceedings and has pursued remedies available under its rules.”

“His children were also aware of the basis of his detention and were actively challenging it before the ICC. Because 𝘩𝘢𝘣𝘦𝘢𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘳𝘱𝘶𝘴 examines whether detention prior to transfer to a court is legal, issuing the writ would serve no practical purpose here,” the SC said in its ruling.
Duterte was arrested by local authorities in March 2025 over an ICC warrant. He is facing three counts of crimes against humanity case for murder and attempted murder.
This case stemmed from the killings in his war on drugs and Davao Death Squad.
However, the SC explained that the dismissal of the petition did not mean that Duterte’s arrest and transfer were necessarily legal or that his rights were not violated.
The High Court said the decision only addressed whether habeas corpus is the proper remedy under the current circumstances.

“The SC explained that any purported violation of Duterte’s rights, including claims for compensation or liability, must be pursued through the appropriate legal proceedings rather than through a petition for habeas corpus,” said the ruling. — Rappler.com

articles.title: Chinese official gets death sentence in spy case, report says
articles.summary: A Chinese official recruited while working abroad was paid more than a million yuan to leak secrets, state-affiliated media reported.

image.caption: The report was published on an account tied to the National Administration of State Secrets Protection Image: Greg Baker/AFP

blocks.text: A Chinese court has sentenced a government official to death for spying for a foreign country, according to a report published Monday by a state-linked social media account.
The official was reportedly convicted of passing on secret information in exchange for payment.
What do we know?
The report was published on an online account run by Gold Wall Press, a publisher tied to the National Administration of State Secrets Protection.
The report named the man only as Ma. The AFP news agency called him a ministerial official, while Reuters described him as an administrative official in China's central apparatus.

According to the report, a foreign operative called "Kailin" recruited Ma while he worked overseas. Kailin first met him regularly on the pretext of learning Chinese. The talks then turned to politically sensitive topics.

A colleague of Kailin's later threatened to tell Chinese authorities about Ma's earlier disclosures unless he cooperated. Later, Ma signed an agreement committing him to confidentiality and loyalty. He received monthly payments and a laptop for sending and receiving intelligence, the report said.
What is the official accused of selling?

Upon returning to China, Ma kept passing on information, sending more than 100 intelligence reports, 35 of them later deemed "top secret," the report said. He was allegedly paid over one million yuan ($150,000, €138,000).
The sentence also includes confiscation of all his personal property.
The report did not say when or where Ma was sentenced, or whether he had already been executed.

Chinese courts rarely publish details of state security cases, but the secrecy regulator and the Ministry of State Security have increasingly publicized them as a warning to officials not to become spies.
"This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call," the report said.
In recent years, the US CIA has published videos in Mandarin seeking informants in China's bureaucracy and military, which Beijing has called a "damning confession."

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Video of priest ‘berating’ impeachment prosecutors is manipulated
articles.summary: The video splices together footage from a June 2022 Mass attended by Duterte and a clip from a July 2026 Mass attended by impeachment prosecutors, with audio taken from a third, unrelated video…

blocks.text: Claim: A video shows a priest criticizing members of the prosecution team in the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte during his homily.
Why we fact-checked this: The claim appears in a November 22 Facebook Reel on the page “The Filipino Connection.”

In the video, the Mass celebrant, who was shown in the first three seconds, can be heard saying: “Tayong mga Katolikong Pilipino, simba nang simba pero corrupt, ‘di ba, simba nang simba pero corrupt, simba nang simba pero magnanakaw… That’s the very reason kasi we are not serious about becoming saints, takot tayo. Ang totoo lahat tayo tinatawag na maging banal, and that is the very reason.”

(We Filipino Catholics, we like going to church but we are corrupt, aren’t we, we like going to church but we are thieves…That’s the very reason, because we are not serious about becoming saints, we are scared. The truth is we are all called to be holy, and that is the very reason.)

The video then cuts to a clip showing several members of the prosecution in Duterte’s impeachment trial: Batangas 2nd District Representative and House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro, Mamamayang Liberal Party-list Representative Leila de Lima, San Juan City Representative Ysabel Maria Zamora, private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan, and Manila 3rd District Representative Joel Chua.
The video’s caption states: “Prosecution sermoned by priest and the guilt in their faces is so profound that each word hit their bodies and kept them in silence.”
As of writing, the video has around 11,800 reactions, 1,800 comments, 6,100 shares, and 612,000 views.

The facts: The video from “The Filipino Connection” is edited. It combines video clips from two separate Catholic Masses with an audio overlay taken from a third, unrelated video, to make it look like the Mass celebrant is addressing the impeachment prosecutors.

The footage in the first three seconds of the video was taken during a Mass at the San Pedro Cathedral in Davao City on June 19, 2022, which was attended by then Vice President-elect Duterte. It was officiated by Archbishop Romulo Valles from the Archdiocese of Davao; he can be seen in the RTVM live stream of the Mass.

The succeeding clip, showing the impeachment trial prosecutors, was taken from a Mass held at the Chapel of the Nativity of the Immaculate Conception Cathedral in Cubao, Quezon City on July 2, 2026 — days before the impeachment trial started on July 6. The prosecutors can be seen in the House of Representatives’ footage of the full Mass.

Although the edited video by “The Filipino Connection” makes it appear that Valles made the remarks calling out the hypocrisy of “corrupt” churchgoers, this statement did not come from him. It was actually made by Fr. Ric Eguia during a November 1, 2026 Mass. The audio from Eguia’s homily was overlaid on the footage of the two separate Masses to create the misleading impression.

Similar posts using the audio from Eguia’s homily have been repurposed in widely circulating videos targeting other public figures. Some use the same 2022 video of Valles, while others feature clips from different Masses. These posts also incorporate unrelated videos of Duterte and President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to create the impression that the priest was berating them.
Previous related fact-checks: Rappler has published numerous fact-checks of videos using fabricated audio overlays:

FACT CHECK: Unrelated audio used in video of crowd mocking VP Sara in Hong Kong
FACT CHECK: ‘Duterte’ chants in video are manipulated, not taken in Netherlands
FACT CHECK: ‘Duterte!’ chants fabricated in video of fitness event in Dubai
FACT CHECK: ‘Duterte!’ chants fabricated in video of Pope Francis’ East Timor visit

blocks.text: Rappler has also fact-checked false claims about church figures. – Percival Bueser/Rappler.com

Percival Bueser is a graduate of Rappler’s fact-checking mentorship program. This fact check was reviewed by a member of Rappler’s research team and a senior editor. Learn more about Rappler’s fact-checking mentorship program here.

articles.summary: A South African fighter pilot and a Ugandan officer are reportedly among those aboard the downed plane.

blocks.text: The Democratic Republic of Congo says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.
The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.
On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a warplane that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.
Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.
The BBC has not independently verified the rebels' claim.
It is also unclear whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one rebels say they shot down.
Uganda's military on Monday denied any involvement.
A statement attributed to army chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba posted on X said: "UPDF had nothing to do with the aircraft that was shot down in Minembwe. We have penalized that company."
The statement did not identify the company or explain what penalty had been imposed.
Gen Kainerugaba later posted that "no Ugandan is allowed to work for mercenary companies in [DR Congo]".
Uganda's denial followed the circulation of a video apparently showing a man being questioned beside the plane's wreckage.
In the footage, the man identifies himself as Ugandan and claims he had been sent by the government. The BBC has not independently verified the video or established the man's identity.
He and the alleged South African pilot are said to be the only other survivors.
South African media outlet Mail & Guardian quoted an FRN spokesperson identifying the pilot as a South African and a "mercenary [who] has no link to the place that he was hired to destroy".
"Unfortunately, we have a multi-country conflict in the eastern DRC," deputy FRN spokesperson Oscar Balinda told the outlet.
The Congolese government has in the past used foreign mercenaries to fight the rebels.
In recent days, fighting between the FRN and the government has intensified with the rebel group accusing the government of targeting heavily populated areas.
The rebels control large areas of eastern DR Congo, including the major city of Goma, after major territorial advances last year.
Aid agencies say the violence is increasingly disrupting healthcare services.
Over the weekend, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières said fighting in North Kivu had forced some of its teams to temporarily suspend outreach activities.
The fighting has also affected the response to the Ebola outbreak, with many health workers trapped, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The epicentre of the outbreak is in eastern DR Congo, which has been wracked by conflict for many decades, with some affected areas under rebel control.

articles.title: What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?
articles.summary: Earth's atmosphere offers protection from a nuclear blast in space, but satellites are more exposed. We explain how radiation could damage them, why the effects can linger and what protection is…

image.caption: The US detonated the weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above Earth, creating an artificial aurora visible from HawaiiImage: U.S. Air Force 1352nd Photographic Group, Lookout Mountain Station/US Govt. Defense Threat Reduction Agency

blocks.text: A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

In the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.
We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.
What does history teach us?

On the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.
An electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.
How does the physics change in space?

The air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

blocks.caption: The glow over Honolulu lasted about seven minutes, but radiation from the blast damaged satellites months laterImage: US Federal Government/Public Domain

blocks.text: Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.
Which systems would be exposed?

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

But satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.
Is it legal, and could it be detected?
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.
The Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.
Can the US protect itself?

Shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.
AI and satellites: The new nuclear watchdogs?

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no new satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.
Whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.
Could radioactive fallout reach the ground?

Some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.
As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

articles.title: Trump made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after Huang’s return
articles.summary: Asia-Pacific stock markets rise after US president says he ‘convinced’ chipmaker’s board to reinstate CEO

blocks.text: Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from the US president.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them … I made the deal.”

The US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news first reported by the Financial Times.

Nvidia’s shares rocketed by 31.5% on Monday, adding about $950bn to the company’s value. Huang returned to the company’s HQ in Santa Clara, California, receiving a hero’s welcome, with crowds of employees chanting “Jensen, Jensen, Jensen!”

Trump has bought shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m, according to a BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the past two years. He has also sold some of his stake in the company since returning to the presidency, and gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
Huang’s surprising, and controversial, return to run Nvidia – which is at the heart of the global AI boom – prompted a strong rally in Asia-Pacific stock markets on Tuesday.

Stocks soared in Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and Australia, as the AI trade lurched back into life after a tumultuous few months. Taiwan’s TW50 index leapt by 9.5%, while South Korea’s Kospi index jumped by 6.5%, led by the chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics. Japan’s Nikkei gained almost 4%.
after newsletter promotion

That followed a rise on Wall Street on Monday. AI shares have been on a rollercoaster in recent months, amid worries over high debt levels in the sector to fund the AI infrastructure buildout, as well as the prospect of tougher regulation in the US after the Democrats’ victory in the midterm elections.

Ruben Gallego, the Democrat senator from Arizona, posted on X: “We need to investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement. This White House is the most corrupt in history.” He later posted: “Trump may have started the popping of the AI bubble.”
Economists said Huang’s return meant the US Federal Reserve was more likely to raise interest rates, with the prospect of the AI bubble bursting imminently diminishing.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said: “With fears of an AI slowdown receding, it also led markets to price back in a more hawkish path for the Federal Reserve over the months ahead.
“So for the next meeting in December, markets are once again fully pricing in a 25 basis point hike.”
