articles.title: Proposed Beatles attraction on Savile Row faces rooftop gigs ban
articles.summary:
Westminster council to vote on restrictions at planned tourist venue and site of band’s final public concert

The Beatles stunned onlookers when they pitched up on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row…

blocks.text: The Beatles stunned onlookers when they pitched up on the rooftop of 3 Savile Row in London in 1969 for their final public performance, but now Westminster city council is seeking to ban live music being played there ahead of plans to convert the site into a tourist attraction.

On Tuesday, councillors will vote on proposals to turn the Grade-II listed building in Mayfair into a seven-storey “cultural experience and exhibition” commemorating the history and legacy of the Fab Four.

Apple Corps, the intellectual property company established by the Beatles in 1968, re-acquired the building – which was the band’s headquarters between 1968 and 1972 – in May, announcing plans to open it to the public as a visitor attraction in 2027.

Westminster council set out a number of conditions for its approval as a visitor attraction, including terms ensuring any amplified audio would have to be controlled through noise limiters, and imposing a restriction on live music on the rooftop to avoid “unacceptable noise levels”. The installation of a 2-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed.

blocks.caption: Westminster council will vote on the proposed Beatles attraction, described as a ‘cultural experience’, on Tuesday. Photograph: Mark Phillips/Alamy

blocks.text: But the plans have faced opposition from businesses on the street, renowned as the heart of British tailoring. The Savile Row Bespoke Association, an organisation representing the area’s tailors, said the street’s narrow pavements “would lead to dangerous congestion and have a significant negative impact on those who visit and work” there.
Planning officers said the proposed changes clashed with local land use policies, but that the building’s unique connection to the Beatles warranted an exception.

Apple Corps said the attraction, which would include a cafe-bar and an exhibition shop, could attract up to 900 visitors on weekdays and 1,140 visitors at weekends, but the Mayfair Neighbourhood Forum said the number of tourists would “need to be greatly reduced” and requested that the planned attraction be monitored for 12 months before an expansion.

The proposed attraction would feature a re-creation of the studio where the band recorded the album Let it Be, as well as giving fans access to the rooftop where the famous concert took place. Items from the Apple Corps archives would also be on show alongside temporary exhibitions.
Paul McCartney called the plans “terrific”.
“Tourists come to England and … go to Abbey Road, but they can’t go inside [the studios] – it snares up the traffic and the drivers get really annoyed,” he said.
Tom Greene, the chief executive of Apple Corps, said: “Every single day, fans are taking pictures of the outside of 3 Savile Row – but next year they can go in.

blocks.caption: Paul McCartney said the plans for the attraction were ‘terrific’. Photograph: Hoberman Publishing/Alamy

blocks.text: “Even the railings remain the same from that famous day in 1969.”
On 30 January 1969, the Beatles played their last public concert on 3 Savile Row’s rooftop to an audience on the street, before the Metropolitan police arrived and ordered them to reduce the volume.

Over a 42-minute set, the band played songs from the final album they recorded together, Let it Be, including Get Back, Don’t Let Me Down, I’ve Got a Feeling and Dig a Pony, as well as an impromptu jam of the national anthem.
The performance was documented in The Beatles: Get Back (2021), an eight-hour documentary series released by Disney which reworked footage from Michael Lindsay-Hogg’s 1970 film, Let it Be.

articles.title: Trump, Nvidia and power: could we be nearing the end of tech’s Gilded Age?
articles.summary:
Oligarchs believe they’re untouchable – the blue wave offers hope that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon be over

One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after…

blocks.text: One can imagine high-fives all around Nvidia’s boardroom after the board reinstated Jensen Huang to the CEO suite. The market gave the move a fat thumbs-up, boosting Nvidia’s share price by about a third. Shareholders, whose interests the board is meant to represent, are surely happy.

But like Fifa’s controversial decision to defer the one-match suspension of US forward Folarin Balogun after receiving a red card for a foul on Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Tarik Muharemović during the World Cup over the summer, Huang’s absolution might backfire.

Like Balogun, it seems Huang was forgiven following a phone call from someone in the White House, maybe even Donald Trump himself, who apparently told Nvidia’s board there was nothing to worry about in the stories about his sleeping around with a potential Chinese spy, as well as a company employee.

But like the US soccer team, which limped on from Trump’s call to Fifa boss Gianni Infantino demanding Balogun be reinstated only to be thumped by Belgium under a cloud of allegations about misuse of presidential power, Huang’s return is unlikely to build Nvidia’s reputation as a paragon of corporate governance.

It’s hard to know what’s what at this stage. There is perhaps a non-zero possibility that Alice Huang was not sleeping with Jensen. Or maybe the relationship was not, in fact, a honey trap to entangle the middle-aged executive in the service of Xi Jinping’s project to secure Nvidia chips.

Maybe, as Trump attested, there is no national security risk to worry about. “One of the things the board wanted to know is: ‘Is there a national security problem?’” he said. “We said: ‘No, it’s not a problem.’”

Unrealistic though this may seem, consider the alternative: the leader of the most important company of the artificial intelligence era was bamboozled by desire into handing over valuable assets to the nation’s main geopolitical rival. And then, the president of the United States – who happens to own a non-trivial number of Nvidia shares – got him off the hook. It’s funny, once you get past terrifying.

And what’s perhaps most terrifying is what Huang’s peccadillos say about power in the AI age. The observant have noted the parallel with the case of Sam Altman – who was fired by the board of OpenAI only to be reinstated within a couple of weeks following a revolt by investors. This has been attributed to Silicon Valley’s fetishistic embrace of company founders as untouchable geniuses who should be left alone to do their will, in the service of profit and progress.

What’s scariest is that this clutch of self-anointed titans – the Huangs and Altmans, the Musks, Amodeis and Zuckerbergs – truly believe that non-tech rubes should get out of the way as they bring about their revolution, one which they admittedly only vaguely understand but which is likely to bring about large-scale unemployment and other massive dislocations to the planet’s 8 billion-plus humans.

It’s hard to find an appropriate parallel. But perhaps the closest precedent came during the Gilded Age, in the late 19th century. The frontier network technology of the time was the railway. The dominant industrial input was steel. The names were also different: Vanderbilt, Carnegie, Rockefeller, Morgan. But the era also suffered from wanton corporate power.

The oligarchs of the time were also untouchable. They not only held absolute sway over their companies, but bought political power as a matter of course, through lobbying, campaign financing and outright bribes. And they benefited handsomely from government largesse. The massive federal subsidies doled out to Elon Musk’s companies have common lineage with the land grants of millions of acres for railroad companies to grow.

Corruption ran rampant. As President Rutherford B Hayes wrote in his diary, echoing Abraham Lincoln’s Gettysburg address: “This is a government of the people, by the people, and for the people no longer. It is a government of corporations, by corporations, and for corporations.” Inequality soared. In 1913, the richest 1% of taxpayers drew almost 18% of the nation’s income and held nearly 40% of the nation’s wealth – similar shares to what they reap and hold today.

The Gilded Age provides us with one reason to believe that the masters of Silicon Valley may be brought to heel: after all, it ended. The Progressive Era that followed in the early 20th century brought about the first federal income tax, antitrust law and a raft of government regulations. Election reforms curbed the power of political machines. A salaried bureaucracy – of the type that Musk’s Doge tried to eviscerate – emerged to reduce bribery. By the late 1970s, the richest 1% hoarded somewhat less than a quarter of the nation’s wealth.

Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections offers a promise that the rampant corruption of the Trump era may soon end. Huang is already set to testify before Congress over the scandal. Maybe companies and their executives will be held accountable for their actions. Maybe the Trump-era notion that the leaders of exceptional companies like Nvidia should be left to do their will is replaced by a focus on their corporate responsibility.
One thing is certain. Trump, thankfully, is soon to lose the ability to change the world with a phone call.

items: Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

articles.title: Palace: No agreed terms, timeline yet for PH-US trade deal
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has yet to agree on the terms of the trade deal announced by United States President Donald Trump during his state visit to the Philippines, Malacañang said on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 3:52pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has yet to agree on the terms of the trade deal announced by United States President Donald Trump during his state visit to the Philippines, Malacañang said on Tuesday.
Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the two countries had yet to finalize the agreement, including its timeline.
"Wala pang terms (There are no terms that the President has agreed to yet)” Castro said in a press briefing.
"Pinag-usapan lang po ay bilisan kung ano man transaction na maaaring mangyari, bilisan ang pagkatrabaho mula sa representative ng Pilipinas at sa representative ng US," she added.
(The discussion was only about expediting any transactions that may take place and speeding up the work between Philippine and US representatives.)
Trump earlier announced that the Philippines would import 100% of its agricultural products and energy requirements from the US starting Jan. 1 next year.
However, Castro said there was no definite timeline for the trade deal as Cabinet members had yet to submit their recommendations.
She explained that the agreement would give the Philippines the option to source commodities from other suppliers.
"Ang lahat po na gagawin na transaction ay makakabuti, kung di man makakabuti pareho sa dalawang bansa, makakabuti ito dapat sa Pilipinas," Castro said.
(Every transaction that will be made should be beneficial. If it is not beneficial to both countries, it should at least benefit the Philippines.)
Castro said the Philippines would remain free to choose its suppliers based on what would be most beneficial to the country.

"Depende sa situasyon. Kung saan mas makakabuti sa bansa natin, yun po ang gagawin ng Pangulo. Halimbawa yung dati nating pinagkukunan ng source, mas mataas o hindi na available o mahirap pasukin, talagang maghahanap ang Pangulo ng bagong source," she added.

(It depends on the situation. The President will choose whatever is best for the Philippines. For example, if our previous source is more expensive, no longer available or difficult to access, the President will look for a new source.)

In a media briefing following the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, Marcos clarified Trump's claim that the Philippines had agreed to source all its agricultural and energy supplies exclusively from the US.
Marcos said the Philippines instead wanted to diversify its sources of basic commodities, which was why it had opened its markets to the US.

“The way I put it is that if you are standing on one foot, sa isa ka lang umaasa, madaling magka problema (if you are relying on only one source, you can easily run into problems)," the President said.
"Kapag marami kang naaasahan, kahit magka problema ng isa, pwede ka pang tumakbo duon sa mga iba. And that's why the trade deal is important,” he added.
(If you have several sources to rely on, even if one encounters a problem, you can turn to the others. And that's why the trade deal is important.)— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Campaigners urge Albanese government to reject ‘climate bomb’ coalmine expansion after Cop31
articles.summary: Hunter Valley Operations expansion in New South Wales would allow additional 430m tonnes of coal to be extracted and burned
articles.byline: Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: Climate campaigners are urging the Albanese government to heed a “line in the sand” warning on fossil fuels issued by dozens of countries at a UN climate summit and refuse a massive coalmine expansion planned in New South Wales.

A proposed agreement at the Cop31 negotiations in Turkey failed after a list of nations – including European Union members, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize – said they would not support it unless it included an explicit statement that the world needed to transition away from fossil fuels.
Activists said the government’s position on fossil fuels in a changing world would be soon tested when it decided whether to approve the Hunter Valley Operations expansion.
The project that would extend open-cut mining by 19 years at the site to 2045 and allow an additional 430m tonnes of coal to be extracted and burned.
The companies behind the development, Glencore and Yancoal, estimated it could lead to 800m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions, mostly when the coal is burned overseas.
The Australian Conservation Foundation (ACF) said it would be “reckless” for the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, to approve the proposal.

“Australia is already one of the world’s largest exporters of climate-heating fossil fuels. What we export as coal and gas comes back as bushfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts,” ACF’s head of advocacy, Gavan McFadzean, said.

The expansion was approved by the New South Wales planning commission in September after it heard from workers, unions, climate organisations, scientists and people around the state who had experienced harm as a result of the climate crisis.
The commission ruled that the climate damage caused by the expansion was “outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW”.

A final decision under federal nature laws now rests with Watt. The national environmental protection agency completed a report making a recommendation about the development earlier this month. It has not been released.

Some longtime observers of UN climate meetings said the results of this year’s Cop31 were a sign that countries were prepared to stand up to fossil fuel interests and block a consensus unless it acknowledged action was needed to reduce on coal, oil and gas, the main causes of the climate crisis.
Earlier this year, nearly 60 national governments were represented at a separate conference in Colombia focused on how to reduce reliance on fossil fuels.

Speaking after the Cop31 summit, the climate change minister, Chris Bowen, who led negotiations at the talks, said he “would have been happy with transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support”. Those opposed to it included Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-rich states.
after newsletter promotion

The head of research and investigations at the Lock the Gate Alliance, Georgina Woods, said the outcome of the UN talks was “a global reflection of a dynamic that we will see coming to a head politically here in Australia”.
She said the Hunter valley Operations coalmine was “a huge coalmine with enormous global warming consequences, and it should be refused”.

“Leaders have preferred to avoid getting stuck into the heart of the issue, that global warming is being driven by the burning of coal, oil, and gas,” she said. “There is a use-by date on that tactic and we’re living through it.

“As people everywhere suffer mounting impacts from the global warming that is caused by mining and burning coal, oil and gas, they will become less and less willing to accept that those industries should keep on being protected when everyone else is paying the price for their pollution.”

Naomi Hodgson, from Rising Tide, a grassroots climate group that holds an annual “people’s blockade” at the coal port of Newcastle, said “to make true on nice words about Pacific solidarity and climate action, the Albanese government must immediately reject” the Hunter valley development, which she described as a “climate bomb”.
A federal government spokesperson said “the decision-making process is still under way and it would be inappropriate to make further comment”.
Hunter Valley Operations declined to comment.

articles.title: Exiled leader Sheikh Hasina plans to return to Bangladesh on Dec. 16
articles.summary: After two years of exile in India, ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has set a return date to Bangladesh. She was sentenced to death in absentia last year over a brutal crackdown that left hundreds…

image.caption: Hasina has been living in an undisclosed location in India since her ouster from BangladeshImage: Daniel Leal-Olivas/AFP/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return to her country on December 16 after two years of exile in India, according to her spokesperson.
That's despite the Bangladeshi government saying she can only return from the neighboring nation through extradition.
"Hasina is a convicted criminal; a fugitive terrorist," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's minister of state for ⁠foreign affairs, ​told Reuters.
"She can only return home by extradition treaty; in handcuffs, and under ​strict surveillance."
Hasina, however, urged current Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her return on the national airline.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5th, 2024, she now calls upon the Government to arrange for ‌her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," the spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said in a ‌statement.
"Having ​exiled her contrary to the Constitution under such circumstances, it is now the responsibility of the government to make possible her return to Bangladesh on Victory Day on December 16th."
December 16 is the anniversary of the end of Bangladesh's 1971 liberation war with Pakistan.
Hasina faces death penalty at home
Hasina, having been sentenced in absentia by a Bangladeshi court last year, faces the death penalty on returning home.
She was ousted by angry protesters in 2024 amid a deadly government crackdown that killed around 1,400 people, according to the UN.
Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back. She has also denied ordering the crackdown.

blocks.caption: Hasina had previously said she would return to Bangladesh but without giving a specific dateImage: Anushree Fadnavis/REUTERS

blocks.text: Earlier this year, Hasina had vowed to return to Bangladesh while speaking at a correspondents' event in New Delhi via live audio feed.
"I know that they may put me in jail, or they may kill me, or anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she said. "Fear cannot decide my duty to the people," she had said then.
This, however, is the first time she has set a date, setting the stage for potential legal disputes.
India did not immediately comment on the set return date.

In April, the Foreign Ministry said it was examining Bangladesh's request to ​extradite her and that it wanted ‌to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties."

articles.title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
articles.summary:
A campaign securing the landmark return to India of ancestral remains taken during British colonial rule has opened a wider conversation about restitution

The lacerating legacy of…

blocks.text: The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects.
For almost 80 years, human remains were displayed on crowded glass shelves at Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University, one of the world’s most celebrated institutions.

Many of them were, in fact, skeletal remains taken from Nagaland brought to the museum by two British colonial administrators, John Henry Hutton and James Philip Mills between 1910 and 1940. Now, after six years of consultations, negotiations and a concerted effort to build consensus across Naga communities, 39 skeletal remains are finally coming home. In early November, the museum handed custodianship to a Naga delegation of leaders and scholars. The repatriated remains include those of two children, a woman and a village chief.

“This is the first such repatriation of human remains to India,” Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist and professor at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told me. She had contacted the Pitt Rivers Museum in 2020 after reading in the Guardian that the museum was removing human remains from public display following an ethical review, setting the repatriation process in motion. In a statement, the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven, acknowledged that it has been a “long journey”, adding that “hope is possible as we work towards reconciliation and healing”.

blocks.caption: Members of the Naga delegation in Oxford, where the university transferred custodianship. Photograph: FNR RRaD Pictures

blocks.text: The review was part of a broader reassessment of the museum’s display practices and how it presented human remains from communities across the world. Among its most contentious displays were the shrunken heads known as tsantsa, from the Shuar people in South America. Pitt Rivers – one of the world’s leading anthropology and ethnography museums – has acknowledged that its display reinforced racist stereotypes about the culture. The Naga remains were displayed alongside artefacts and human remains from a number of communities, including from Nigeria and Papua New Guinea.

Naga academics have challenged the perception that the remains were exclusively associated with the practice of headhunting. While Naga warriors traditionally collected the heads of enemies killed in raids, the anthropologists say that British collectors acquired Naga human remains under duress during colonial expeditions.

For the Naga community, that was just the beginning of a long journey. India, unlike countries such as Australia, Canada and the US, has no national laws for the repatriation of Indigenous ancestral remains, says Kikon. “We had to ensure the process was community-led, in the absence of a policy and make sure the focus remained on healing and reconciliation. It was all unprecedented.”

The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a collective working toward peace and reconciliation among Naga Indigenous communities, facilitated the repatriation, and a voluntary research group, Recover, Restore and Decolonise (RRaD), was formed to build wider community awareness. Its volunteers travelled to urban centres and villages, talking with students, elders and intergenerational audiences about the human remains kept at the museum and what the community wanted to do with them.

The museum still has around 178 objects that contain, or may contain, human hair. It also has 6,500 Naga objects, including clothing items, weapons, vessels and musical instruments, many from Mills and Hutton, while some items, like weapons, were bought from auction houses. “The Pitt Rivers Museum has one of the largest collections of Naga objects, artefacts and human remains in the world. What we have focused on for now is the skeletal remains, but this is only a first step in thinking more broadly about these collections,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at Edinburgh University.

The question of restitution of Indian artefacts and cultural heritage items has long occupied a prominent place in public discourse. At its heart is the Koh-i-noor diamond, which passed through Mughal, Persian and Afghan hands before Britain wrested it from the 10-year-old king, Maharaja Duleep Singh. Today, it is part of the British crown jewels, a symbol of the plunder of the empire and, for many in India, a theft that continues to rankle. Last year, an Indian parliamentary committee recommended establishing a dedicated heritage recovery taskforce to pursue the return of cultural objects held abroad, particularly those taken during the colonial period.

In the case of the human remains, the question is about the right to honour the ancestors and give them a dignified resting place. “How we imagine a shared future depends on how we understand our history. We have to look back and make sense of the past in order to think about the kind of future we want to create,” Longkumer told me.
“The Naga repatriation addresses a very deep colonial violence,” Kikon says. “It is about the dehumanisation where the remains of human beings were stored in museums and exhibited as exotic objects.”

The return prompted Kikon to reflect on the contradiction between the longstanding reverence for Oxford University by Indians, many of whom have aspired to study there, and the institution’s history of exhibiting the remains of their ancestors. “Repatriation is not just about bringing back bones. It was about starting a process of deep introspection,” she says. “Ultimately, it leaves us with a greater responsibility to reflect on how we live our lives.”
The remains will be buried at Naga Solidarity Park in Kohima, the capital of Nagaland.

A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Barefoot College brings solar-powered lighting to rural areas. Photograph: Rebecca Conway/Getty Images

blocks.text: Writer Gayatri Rangachari Shah, a founding member of the Women Leadership Circle, recommends an inspiring model of rural development. “If there is an institution that captures an alternative vision of India, it’s the Barefoot College in Rajasthan. Set up by Sanjit ‘Bunker’ Roy in 1972, it has spent more than five decades putting rural communities at the centre of their own development. Its Solar Mamas programme has enabled women of all ages who had never been to school to learn to make and install solar lights. Its other initiatives include digital learning centres for young women, night schools for those working during the day, menstrual-friendly toilets in government schools, rainwater harvesting, waste management and recycling.
Roy died on 10 November but he passed on his work to a younger team.”

blocks.caption: GTA VI has brought Disco Jazz to new audiences. Photograph: YouTube

blocks.text: Grand Theft Auto VI, billed as the biggest cultural event of the year, has smashed sales records. It has also helped propel a little-known 1982 Indian disco track to global fandom. Aaj Shanibar by the Bengali singer Rupa Biswas features on Worldwide FM, one of the radio stations in the game.

The song was part of an album called Disco Jazz that Biswas recorded during a visit to her brother in Canada. The album never made a splash and faded into obscurity, but years later her son discovered the track had found a following in DJ sets and was reissued by the US label Numero Group. Now, with GTA VI, the song has reached a generation who were not even born when the original was released 44 years ago.

articles.title: Supreme Court junks bid to question Duterte's arrest, ICC transfer
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has dismissed the consolidated petitions for habeas corpus challenging the arrest and transfer of former President Rodrigo Duterte to the International Criminal Court.

blocks.text: November 24, 2026 | 3:30pm
Former President Rodrigo Duterte boards a chartered plane that is destined for The Hague, Netherlands.
Contributed photo via News5; former NICA director Alex Paul Monteagudo via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has dismissed the consolidated petitions for habeas corpus challenging the arrest and transfer of former President Rodrigo Duterte to the International Criminal Court.
According to the Supreme Court, Philippine courts can no longer enforce the writ since Duterte is already detained in The Hague, the Netherlands.
Voting 9-4, the high court's en banc denied the petitions filed by Duterte's children — Sebastian, Veronica and Paolo — on their father's behalf.
The high court held that a writ of habeas corpus is strictly a domestic remedy that cannot be enforced beyond Philippine territory or against an international tribunal.

"Significantly, [Duterte] is not just beyond the Court's coercive powers, but also stands accused before an international tribunal that has assumed jurisdiction over his person," the Supreme Court said.
The high court also pointed out that Duterte is already actively participating in ICC proceedings and pursuing legal remedies there, rendering a domestic writ futile.

Furthermore, because the transfer had already been completed, the Philippine officials named in the petitions no longer hold custody or control over him and cannot be ordered to produce or release him.
Legality of arrest left open
The Supreme Court clarified that dismissing the petitions on mootness does not validate the legality of Duterte's arrest and surrender, nor does it mean his constitutional rights were not violated.
Rather, the ruling strictly addresses whether habeas corpus remains a viable remedy.

articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has dismissed consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte, ruling that they have become moot and that Philippine courts…

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 3:28pm

The Supreme Court (SC) has dismissed consolidated habeas corpus petitions challenging the arrest of former President Rodrigo Duterte, ruling that they have become moot and that Philippine courts cannot enforce the writ because he is already in the custody of another state.
In a press release issued Tuesday, the SC En Banc denied the consolidated petitions filed by Duterte’s children, Sebastian, Veronica and Paolo Duterte.
A day after Duterte’s arrest in March 2025, his children separately filed petitions for habeas corpus, a legal remedy used to challenge unlawful detention and seek a person’s release.

“The Office of the Solicitor General (OSG) argued that the petitions had become moot, or no longer needed to be resolved, because a writ of habeas corpus issued by Philippine courts cannot be enforced outside the country,” the SC said in its press release.
“It also maintained that the arrest complied with the Philippines’ international obligations,” it added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: What China's Xi could take away from Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
articles.summary: Huang being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has riveted the world - including China, where it has become the top trending post on Weibo, the country's biggest social media platform.

Most users are pleased to see the return of the influential billionaire, who declared that he loved China, before videos appeared online of him eating noodles and drinking milk tea during a visit in May. Some wondered why - in the video of him returning to Nvidia's headquarters - he is not wearing one of his leather jackets.
But to many, Huang's return, which is being dubbed one of the greatest U-turns of all time, seems like a vindication for China.
That's probably how Xi Jinping sees it too.

Beijing has dismissed claims that one of the women who had an affair with Jensen Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its version of the CIA, as a spy. Chinese state media has also framed the spy saga as a smear campaign orchestrated by China hawks in Washington. The Global Times, a Communist Party mouthpiece, described it as a "witch hunt".
Now the White House, and President Donald Trump himself, have said Huang poses no national security threat, although investigations into the spy allegations are still ongoing.
Xi will have learned many lessons from this scandal, especially about Trump's pressure points.

For one, the fact that Huang's reappointment came so soon after Xi's meetings last week with Trump in Shenzhen could be read as a sign that direct engagement is an effective way to influence Washington.
Trump has said the two men discussed Huang, but did not elaborate further. Beijing has not commented.

The episode has also reinforced the view among Chinese officials that there are two camps in Washington: those in favour of restricting Chinese access to cutting edge tech to protect US national security, and those, like Huang, who believe that such restrictions will not limit Beijing's ambitions.

Huang has repeatedly argued that US export controls will force Chinese firms like Huawei to build independent alternatives - all the while shutting American companies out of the world's second-largest economy.
But him being back at the helm of Nvidia is no guarantee of relief for Beijing.

Rather, the sale of advanced chips will remain a key point of contention between the US and China, especially as the two sides try to reach a trade deal before another Trump-Xi meeting, which is expected in December.
Already new rules are being put in place that will worry Beijing.

The US Bureau of Industry and Security is tightening restrictions by targeting not only the direct export of advanced chips to China, but also Chinese firms' ability to use computing power in data centres overseas.

The measures are designed to close potential loopholes that allow Chinese companies to access advanced Nvidia and AMD chips through cloud providers operating in third countries, including Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand.
China has yet to react with measures of its own. But investors will be watching closely for any escalation which could weigh on US equity markets.
And having seen how eager Trump is to keep things stable, Xi may see this as leverage.

He now knows Trump is so worried about the stock market that he is prepared to intervene in the HR decisions of the world's biggest company. The president has also personally invested in Nvidia, although the White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
China has already used its considerable chokehold over the world's rare earth metals to bring the US to the negotiating table over trade.

If Washington restricts chip exports and Beijing retaliates, that could be the start of a cycle that has a profound effect on the stock market because American companies, from car makers to defence firms to chip manufacturers, all rely on rare earths.
What China has realised is that more trouble lies ahead as it tries to build what it describes as a "constructive strategic relationship" with the US.
Trump's tariffs are no longer at the heart of that tussle. Now it's about control of critical technology and minerals which could, in turn, affect each side's military influence and economic power.
What happens next will depend on how the Jensen Huang saga unfolds because it is far from over.
Huang is set to testify before Congress next month, and come January, a Democrat-controlled Congress will raise the pressure. Even some Republican lawmakers have made clear they want answers.
Arkansas senator Tom Cotton wrote on X that the Nvidia controversy "is just the tip of the iceberg and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back".

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI engineer vibecoded better bugs to record meetings – court filing
articles.summary: Federal prosecutors are seeking to prevent ex-OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan from being released prior to his trial on a charge of illegally intercepting conversations

blocks.text: BEHIND THE BUG? A man described as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device had been placed at a conference room in OpenAI offices, in a still image from surveillance video included in a charging document after US federal agents the man and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device, in San Francisco, California, USA, October 5, 2026.
Department of Justice/Handout via Reuters
Federal prosecutors are seeking to prevent ex-OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan from being released prior to his trial on a charge of illegally intercepting conversations

items: Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan was arrested for allegedly planting a hidden bug to record office conversations, including meetings with foreign government representatives.
Alfozan has pleaded not guilty to charges of illegally intercepting conversations and is seeking release on a $1 million bond, which prosecutors oppose.
Prosecutors claim Alfozan's recordings contain confidential trade secrets and have linked his communications with Saudi officials to his efforts to record OpenAI meetings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested in October and accused of planting a hidden bug to record office conversations, was said to have recorded a number of meetings including one held with foreign government representatives, federal prosecutors said in a court filing.
The New York Times reported on Monday, November 23, that Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and a permanent US resident, was charged with one count of illegally intercepting conversations.

Alfozan pleaded not guilty, and a hearing for his release is scheduled for November 24. He has also asked the federal judge to allow him to be released on a $1-million bond. Prosecutors opposed Alfozan’s request to be released from jail before his trial begins in January.

Prosecutors said Alfozan used OpenAI’s Codex vibecoding application to improve his hidden recording device by adding voice-detection and using Codex to organize the recordings in Dropbox. The Codex account was in his wife’s name, though she has not been accused of wrongdoing.

OpenAI said many of the recordings kept by Alfozan either held confidential trade secrets, such as meetings with OpenAI customers, or were identified as having material protected by attorney-client privilege.
Prosecutors did not say in the filing that Alfozan had shared the recordings. “What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation.”
David Rizk, Alfozan’s lawyer, argued in a filing last week that the case was less serious than prosecutors suggested.
Rizk called Alfozan “an overly curious tinkerer,” and said the majority of recordings on Alfozan’s computer “apparently contain just random noise and silence.”

Prosecutors, for their part, outlined the timeline of the recordings, which spanned 15 folders dated September 8 to 28. It also had recordings of meetings held on 12 days in an executive conference room, with one file titled “1200-sovereign-bilateral-briefing-sep22.” The filing did not identify any foreign government.

Prosecutors added that Alfozan took photos of the printings of a confidential term sheet for a “strategic partnership” between OpenAI and another company early on October 5. That same day, a hidden camera recorded him checking behind the television where OpenAI’s security team previously found the planted listening device.
Alfozan was also said to have had contact with Saudi officials, according to the filing.

On October 6, a member of the Saudi royal family sent Alfozan a link to Echelon, a Riyadh-based AI company. Alfozan was asked, “Time to move back to KSA and join us?” Alfozan replied that he might return “after the IPO” of OpenAI, which is slated for next year.
He apparently spoke with the Saudi official through WhatsApp for 16 minutes and exchanged messages with Saudi communications ministry officials, including the minister in August, and September.
Prosecutors argued the timing of his Saudi discussions and his travel plans “appears to match the timing of his efforts to record OpenAI meetings.”
Alfozan’s lawyers said the trip was planned for paternity leave, as his wife was pregnant.
Magistrate Judge Alex Tse, who rejected the original bid for Alfozan’s release, will preside the hearing on Tuesday.
Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release if he is convicted in the January trial. .– Rappler.com

articles.title: UK disability benefit cuts risk worsening youth destitution, research warns
articles.summary:
Joseph Rowntree Foundation report says millions could be left unable to regularly afford everyday basics

Cuts to disability benefits are likely to increase the risks of destitution faced by…

blocks.text: Cuts to disability benefits are likely to increase the risks of destitution faced by young people and leave millions of people unable to regularly afford everyday basics such as food, shelter and clothing, according to new research.

Destitution is “becoming the norm” with about 3.8 million people, including 1 million children, experiencing the most extreme form of financial hardship in the UK last year, says the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

A quarter of people in destitution had no income at all, while a further 58% reported net incomes after paying rent of less than £90 a week, the research found, with those affected increasingly reliant on crisis services such as food banks.

Although the research was completed before the recent Milburn report’s proposals to scrap disability benefits for under-25s, it notes the current low rates of benefits mean young people are already at disproportionately high risk of destitution.

The government is to publish a white paper in the new year setting out its responses to the Milburn report, as well as Tuesday’s expected Timms review of the main disability benefit, personal independence payment (Pip).

Disability campaigners and poverty charities have made it clear they will oppose any attempts to remove disability benefits for under-25s, arguing that financial insecurity has a negative impact on health and makes it harder for people to get a job.

People are defined as destitute if they have been unable to afford two or more of the six basic necessities over the past month: shelter (ie, not sleeping rough); food; heating; lighting; clothing and footwear; and basic toiletries.

The destitution research, by academics at Heriot-Watt University in Edinburgh, said historically Pip – which supports people with the extra costs of disability – played a “critical role” in helping disabled people to escape extreme financial hardship.

“It is therefore imperative that any future changes to benefits following the Timms and Milburn reviews should ensure that disability benefits reach people with health conditions and/or disabilities with the greatest need for additional financial support, and without undue delay,” the report says.
“This is especially important for disabled people whose income is so low that they risk destitution,” it adds.

It notes that halving universal credit health payments in April to all new claimants was likely to “significantly reduce the incomes of some households at risk of destitution”. Last week the Milburn review recommended this benefit be removed for all under-25s.

About 61% of destitute people report a disability or long-term health condition, and while the public debate centres on increased numbers of people claiming disability benefits, the research found 37% of destitute people with life-limiting conditions were not receiving disability benefits.

“What is particularly disturbing is the evidence that destitution is becoming a more persistent experience, with people repeatedly needing crisis support simply to meet their basic needs,” said the report co-author Prof Suzanne Fitzpatrick of Heriot-Watt University.
after newsletter promotion

“We are no longer looking at a temporary spike in hardship. Millions of people remain unable to afford the basic necessities needed to live, and there is something profoundly wrong when that becomes an enduring feature of life for so many in the UK.”

Greater London had the highest rate of extreme hardship, with two in every 100 households experiencing destitution. The UK local authority areas most affected were Newham, Westminster, Manchester, Tower Hamlets and Hounslow.
Groups most likely to experience destitution were single working-age adults, disabled people, people from minoritised ethnic communities, and migrants.

“Without action, we risk destitution becoming the norm for millions in the UK. Behind these stark figures are real people who don’t have what they need to survive – food, shelter, basic toiletries and clothing,” said Julian Hartley, the group chief executive of the Joseph Rowntree Foundation.

A government spokesperson said: “This government is turning the tide on poverty after years of rising hardship. Household incomes have risen 5% in real terms, food bank usage has fallen and the decision to remove the two-child limit will lift 450,000 children out of poverty by the end of this parliament.”

“We will consider the findings of the Milburn and Timms reviews together and set out the next steps on our reforms in the coming weeks, but we are clear that there will always be a strong safety net for those who need it.”

articles.title: Bangladesh's ex-PM Sheikh Hasina says she plans to return on 16 December
articles.summary: Hasina has spoken several times of her desire to return, but this is the first time she has set a date.

blocks.text: Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.

But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule. She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ​request for comment. In April, ​the ministry said it was ⁠examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.

What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.

"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.

The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.

Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.

The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.

"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.

India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

articles.title: Sports whistleblowers protected under proposed laws amid Australian cricket ball tampering saga
articles.summary:
Amendments to government bill by Coalition and Greens would establish protections for those reporting wrongdoing in sport

  • Get our

blocks.text: Whistleblowers reporting corruption or misconduct in sport would be protected under draft laws put forward by the Coalition and the Greens, in response to the Australian Test cricket ball-tampering scandal.

The South Africa tour of 2018 is back in the national spotlight after the publication of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography earlier this month, in which he claimed players had used sandpaper to tamper with the ball before the third Test on the infamous tour, and that the entire squad knew about the practice.
The opposition and the minor party have both put forward separate amendments to Labor’s draft legislation that seeks to criminalise particular behaviour that undermine the integrity of sport.
The government’s bill, first introduced to parliament in August, well before Khawaja’s claims were published, is before the Senate and is expected to be voted on this week.
The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, has called on Labor to establish a dedicated whistleblower protection scheme for sport.
This would accompany an “independent reporting channel” outside sporting bodies and enforceable protection against reprisal.
“Fans deserve to know the games they love are clean, and athletes, coaches and support staff deserve to know they won’t lose their careers for telling the truth,” Shoebridge said.
“We’re calling on parties across the parliament to support this move.”
The Liberal senator Michaelia Cash has also circulated proposed protection for people reporting corrupt conduct.
A whistleblower would qualify for protection if information is communicated to law enforcement, a sporting body, or Sport Integrity Australia and was provided in “good faith”.
A court could also make an order to reinstate a person to their position or one at a comparable level, if they experienced reprisal due to their disclosure.
This covers employees who are expelled or suspended from a club or competition, or are not selected or otherwise removed from a previously held role or in a team, club or competition.
The government’s national sport integrity draft legislation introduces new offences to criminalise certain behaviour, such as the manipulation of a sporting event.

“Recognising that a fair, safe and strong sport sector, free from corruption, is vital to the safety and credibility of sports, their participants, and to Australia’s credibility as a participant in the international sporting arena,” the memorandum of the bill reads.
after newsletter promotion
Human Rights Law Centre’s whistleblower project associate legal director, Kieran Pender, said sport is a “missing piece” in Australia’s whistleblowing legal system.
“It is a major integrity gap that people who raise concerns with Sport Integrity Australia or other relevant regulators are not protected,” he said.
“The Albanese government should seize this opportunity to improve whistleblower protections and better support people who expose wrongdoing in sport. That will ensure a fairer game for all.”
Australian cricketers Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were given significant bans as a result of the ball-tampering scandal.
Warner, Bancroft and reserve bowler Chadd Sayers have publicly supported Khawaja’s account, while current Test captain Pat Cummins refuted the claims in a 70-minute press conference in Sydney.
Cricket Australia has since announced an independent “forum” for players and staff to share their version of events to provide a “circuit-breaker”.

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Tuesday picked up a tennis racket and led the ceremonial serve with the sport's rising star Alex Eala during her homecoming event in Pasig City.
Marcos and Eala gamely engaged in rallies that drew cheers from the audience at the Pasig Elementary School.
Up next was Education Secretary Sonny Angara, who had a longer rally against Eala.
The Filipino tennis sensation also conducted a tennis demonstration during the event, teaching young athletes the basics of tennis.
Olympic gold medal weightlifter Hidilyn Diaz and former world No. 2 pole vaulter EJ Obiena were also present during the activity.
During her homecoming, the Department of Education and Milo Philippines conferred the Gawad Sulo ng Simula at Tagumpay to Eala for her outstanding achievement.
Eala has climbed to a career-high ranking of No. 15 in the world, capping her 2026 season with a runner-up finish at the Hong Kong Tennis Open.
In his speech, Marcos praised Eala for serving as a reminder for her countrymen to be proud of being Filipinos.
"Pagka may kausap kaming hindi Pilipino, 'Ayan ang mga Pilipino. Akala ninyo kayo lang ang magaling? Magagaling din ang Pinoy,' and you make us proud to be Filipino," he added.
(When we talk to foreigners we say, 'Look at Filipinos. You thought you're the only ones who excel? Filipinos also excel,' and Alex you make us proud to be Filipino.)

articles.title: Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy
articles.summary: According to a study by the Körber Foundation, a growing number of Germans now oppose providing military aid to Ukraine. The majority also believes that Germany should take a neutral position between…

image.caption: Chancellor Friedrich Merz has insisted on German support for Ukraine's war effort against RussiaImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

Long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

In the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents said they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.
Growing numbers of Germans oppose international engagement

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points."
Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.
No longer a majority in favor of military aid to Ukraine

The most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.
As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer said. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine."
The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).
Overwhelming majority wants Germany to remain neutral between the US and China

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

This may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers."

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.
"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," said Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.
If Europe wants independence, why does it keep turning to the US?
Should Germany always stand by Israel? Now only a third agree

One issue that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

This may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?"

The results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Malaysia to send thousands of migrants back to Myanmar as PM acknowledges junta’s ‘atrocities’
articles.summary:
Prime minister Anwar Ibrahim’s announcement comes days after the ICJ found Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya minority

Malaysia says it will send thousands of migrants and…

blocks.text: Malaysia says it will send thousands of migrants and refugees back to Myanmar, despite acknowledging that many asylum seekers in the country had been victims of “atrocities” carried ​out by the junta in Naypyidaw.
The announcement comes just days after the UN’s highest court ruled Myanmar had committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

Malaysia’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim, said on Tuesday that the deportations were in line with advice from the international court of justice (ICJ), which was “to guarantee a safe and dignified return” for those fleeing persecution, and his country had not abandoned its principles of upholding the rights of the people of Myanmar.
The UN has previously warned that migrants sent back to Myanmar could face a dangerous homecoming.

It is unclear how many Rohingya, a Muslim minority group, are among those facing deportation. However, the Rohingya make up two-thirds of the 190,000 Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, according to the UN. Many of the Rohingya escaped to Malaysia during a brutal military crackdown in 2017.

Anwar acknowledged that many asylum seekers in Malaysia were “victims of atrocities carried ​out by the Myanmar regime”, but said Malaysia could ‌no longer afford to host refugees. Hoping for them to be resettled in third countries had not worked, he said.

Many in Malaysia have grown increasingly frustrated by ‌the presence of refugees in the country, saying that hosting them has become a financial burden and a security risk, with a rise in anti-migrant sentiment in the country.

On Tuesday Anwar told Malaysia’s parliament that three naval ships would return 1,500 people in December, with an additional 5,303 people flown back by aircraft at the expense of the Myanmar government.
Tuesday’s announcement follows last week’s ICJ ruling in The Hague that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ had never previously found a state responsible for genocide, and the judgment ended a seven-year legal battle that was seen as a critical global test for dealing with the most serious of all state crimes.

The 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military forced more than 700,000 mostly Muslim Rohingya to flee across the border into Bangladesh, arriving with reports of mass killings of adults and children, gang rapes and burnt-down villages.
In its judgment, the ICJ said Myanmar authorities must “allow and facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return” of refugees displaced either within Myanmar or abroad.
In September, Malaysia began sending back a group of about 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched its contested repatriation plan.
Malaysia’s government said in a statement at the time that the repatriation was necessary to resolve the “legacy issue” of foreign asylum seekers in Malaysia – of which it said 95% were from Myanmar.

“This long-standing issue has imposed a significant financial burden on the nation, triggered serious social crises, and created tangible security threats for the Malaysian people,” the statement said.
The UN had urged Malaysia to stop that repatriation, saying nobody should be deported to Myanmar, given the severity of the situation on the ground.
In late October, the Malaysian government said it would seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned were being held in military detention.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: DOJ to review truth body findings on Duterte's drug war
articles.summary: The commission reports that at least 8,320 killings occured during the drug war, based on information culled from news reports, online repositories, religious groups and government records.

blocks.text: November 24, 2026 | 1:52pm

A relative of a victim of an extra-judicial killing attends a memorial mass ahead of All Soul's Day to remember loved ones slain in the government's war on drugs, at the Commission on Human Rights in Manila on Oct. 29, 2021.
AFP / Jam Sta. Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Justice will form a panel to review the cases and data reported by the civil society-led Truth Commission on former President Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs, Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida said on Monday, November 23.
In an interview with ANC, Vida said that the department would look at the entirety of the commission’s report and examine the evidence presented by the group.

“What are the pieces of evidence (they reported)? Are they all testimonial? Are they pieces of object evidence?… We don’t want to file weak cases; if ever it will be filed,” Vida said in a mix of English and Filipino.
The department previously formed a similar panel in 2022, with 52 cases reaching the courts.
Only nine cases resulted in convictions, including that of Kian Delos Santos, a 17-year-old student fatally shot by police officers during an anti-illegal drugs operation in Caloocan.
The Supreme Court affirmed in 2025 the conviction of three police officers involved in the killing of Delos Santos, finding them guilty of murder beyond reasonable doubt.

Officers Arnel Oares, Jeremias Pereda and Jerwin Cruz were ordered to pay the heirs of Delos Santos around P250,000 in damages, in addition to serving their sentence of reclusion perpetua, which carries a prison term of 20 to 40 years.
Duterte’s case at The Hague
According to Vida, the DOJ will also consider how the 8,320 killings in the commission’s registry relate to Duterte’s case before the International Criminal Court.

Duterte, currently detained at the ICC Detention Centre in The Hague, the Netherlands, has been charged with three counts of crimes against humanity of murder linked to his administration’s anti-drug campaign.
The charges are separated by time period and type of killing, meaning prosecutors must prove each count independently.

As of October 2026, Duterte’s case covers 56 incidents, spanning from his time as mayor of Davao City from 2013 to June 2016 and the first two years of his presidency, from July 2016 to September 2018.
Having led the Philippine National Police during the initial and most intensive phase of the anti-drug crackdown, Sen. Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa is also wanted by the ICC.
Dela Rosa, however, remains in hiding and has been absent from Senate sessions since May 2026.
Duterte’s trial before the ICC, meanwhile, opens on Monday, November 30, at 5 p.m.

articles.title: India's 'cockroach' party leader says he was stopped from flying to UK
articles.summary: Saurav Das said that immigration authorities at Delhi airport told him that his passport had been "flagged".

blocks.text: A leader of India's "cockroach" party has said that immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him from flying to the UK, where he was set to attend a series of events.
Saurav Das said he was supposed to board a flight on Tuesday at 01:00 local time (19:30 GMT on Monday) but was told by immigration officers that his passport had been "flagged".
It is not clear yet why Das's passport was flagged. The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.
Das, who rose to prominence in India earlier this year after Gen Z-led protests, said that he had been invited by the Oxford Union to speak about the movement.
He said that he was also scheduled to speak at other universities in Cambridge and Edinburgh.
"Indian students put their heart and soul to organise the events but this anti-intellectual [government] was scared of me going to these prestigious institutions," he wrote on X.
A federal home ministry spokesperson directed the BBC to airport authorities and the Delhi police for comment on Das's allegations.
Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said in a post on X that she and Das had been invited by the Oxford Union but that her visa had been rejected a few days ago.

"The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country," she wrote.
Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.
In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands of people detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.
The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.
There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.
In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.
