articles.title: Marcos to Alex Eala: You remind us to be proud to be Pinoy
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Tuesday praised Filipino tennis sensation Alex Eala for serving as a reminder for her countrymen to be proud of being Filipinos.

blocks.text: Published November 24, 2026 1:00pm
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. on Tuesday praised Filipino tennis sensation Alex Eala for serving as a reminder for her countrymen to be proud of being Filipinos.
Speaking at her homecoming event in Pasig City, Marcos told Eala, "We are not only proud of you, you remind Filipinos to be proud to be Pinoy, just like Hidilyn (Diaz), just like EJ (Obiena)."
Olympic gold medal weightlifter Diaz and former world No. 2 pole vaulter Obiena were also present during the activity.
"Pagka may kausap kaming hindi Pilipino, 'Ayan ang mga Pilipino. Akala ninyo kayo lang ang magaling? Magagaling din ang Pinoy,' and you make us proud to be Filipino," he added.
(When we talk to foreigners we say, 'Look at Filipinos. You thought you're the only ones who excel? Filipinos also excel,' and Alex you make us proud to be Filipino.)
Marcos also led the ceremonial serve at the venue's indoor tennis court, where he gamely engaged Eala, the No. 15 tennis player in the world, in a few friendly rallies that delighted the crowd.
Education Secretary Sonny Angara also tried his hand with the tennis racket against Eala.
Eala followed with a tennis demonstration to the Filipinos in attendance.
Grace in defeat
Marcos reminded the Eala, who was recently nominated as the 2026 Most Improved Player by the Women's Tennis Association (WTA), to take care of her body and avoid injuries to avoid permanent impact.
The President also pointed out that there's "grace" in playing sports.
"Other than injury, everything about sports teaches you good lessons, teaches you discipline, teaches you camaraderie, teaches you grace," Marcos said.
"Why grace? Kapag hindi ka nanalo, puwede mo pa rin lapitan 'yung nakatalo sa iyo and say congratulation na hindi ka nagagalit, hindi ka napipikon," he added.
(Why grace? If you don't win, you can still approach the person who won against you and say congratulations, where you're not angry or upset.)
The 21-year-old has climbed to a career-high ranking of No. 15 as of early November 2026, capping her season with a runner-up finish at the Hong Kong Tennis Open.
Be like Alex
Meanwhile, Angara urged the youth to be like Eala, who not only excels in sports but also finished her education.

"Gayahin natin si Alex Eala na hindi lang magaling on court, magaling din off court dahil alam ko masipag siya mag-aaral kaya naka-graduate siya, kahit na homeschooling siya, binibigyan niya ng oras ang pag-aaral niya despite all the demands of her professional career," Anagara told reporters.

(Be like Alex Eala who is not only good on the court but off the court as well. I know she studies hard that's why she graduated, even though she is homeschooled, she makes time for her studies despite all the demands of her professional career.)
Angara explained that it is important for Athletes to also finish their studies in order the prepare better for their retirement.
DepEd and Milo Philippines conferred the Gawad Sulo ng Simula at Tagumpay to Eala.
Angara said the award recognizes individuals with outstanding achievements.
"Definitely Alex has given a lot pride to the country," Angara said.

"It is really symbolic for Alex because Alex has already done so much for the country by just being Alex Eala and by being an excellent ambassador. So kapag mismong kausap na niya ang mga (So when she talks to) Pilipino on Filipino soil and encouraging them to play tennis, it's very hard to overstate 'yung impact nu'n, grabe," he added. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Ebikes, screens and failing manners pose challenge for Dutch cycling culture
articles.summary:
Awareness campaign reminds public ‘traffic is a team sport’ amid less civility and more collisions on roads

For decades the Netherlands has been famed for its proud cycling culture, with a…

blocks.text: For decades the Netherlands has been famed for its proud cycling culture, with a network of 23,000 miles of bike paths used by everyone from children under eight to adults over 80.

In recent years, however, like so many countries around the world, it has seen a dramatic change in the type of vehicles using those lanes: no longer the preserve of pedal bikes, they are used by all manner of two-wheeled vehicles including electric cargo bikes, thick-tyred “fatbikes”, speed pedelecs, electric scooters and even some micro cars.

Throw smartphones into the mix as well, say critics, and the result is clear: less space, more conflict, less civility and more collisions. According to the Netherlands Institute for Transport Policy Analysis, the annual number of cyclist deaths increased by more than 50% between 2015 and 2025.
What is needed, say some, are new rules of the road (or, at least, path). Last week, the Dutch government sent a bill to parliament proposing mandatory helmets for under-18s on ebikes.

The moves are welcomed by those who feel that things need to change. As one resident, Patrick van den Hoven, wrote in the Amsterdam newspaper Het Parool this month: “Let’s call a spade a spade: [ebikes] are vehicles with a motor, which, as far as I am concerned, we should treat as motor vehicles.”
The city’s bike lanes now resembled “a permanent traffic experiment”, he said, adding: “The bicycle made our country great. It would be a shame if it eventually fell victim to electric progress.”

Another city, Leiden, launched a public awareness campaign earlier this month to remind everyone that “traffic is a team sport”. It has the Netherlands’ highest number bike accidents per head, and cyclist injuries have risen by more than half since 2018.

blocks.caption: Bicycles on the Corn Bridge in Leiden. Photograph: John and Tina Reid/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This campaign aims to say: guys, watch out for one another,” said Julius Terpstra, the deputy mayor for spatial planning and mobility. “We see more people on bikes, more older people on bikes due to the ageing population, and more different vehicles, when once the Netherlands only had the Gazelle [a famed brand of pedal bike]. We see national trends here too: the rise of the electric bike, more telephone use, and also drug use.”

According to Florrie de Pater, a board member of the Fietsersbond Amsterdam cycling union, there has been a notable decline in road manners. “There is less consideration for one another and less empathy among cyclists, perhaps also because we live in an individualistic world where everything has to go fast, fast, fast,” she said.

Romee Nicolai, the bicycle mayor of Amsterdam, believes some people have forgotten that the extensive network of dedicated cycle paths was created after a wave of activism sparked by road deaths in the 1970s.

“People have been cycling for hundreds of years, but we need to acknowledge that this cannot continue if we don’t give it attention,” she said. “You can’t grow plants if you don’t give them attention and water, and it’s the same with cycling. That means public debate, and financial means from government to create a safe cycling environment too.”

Some older people have told her they are too afraid of an accident to get on their bicycles, while one in five children are growing up without a cycling culture. “We need to acknowledge that we are actually losing those cyclists,” Nicolai said.

blocks.caption: Bicycles parked near Amsterdam’s central station. Photograph: Jochen Tack/Alamy

blocks.text: The National Institute for Public Health and the Environment found in a recent study that fewer Dutch young adults were doing the recommended daily amount of movement, partly owing to less general cycling and the rise of the electric bike.

Jasper Reenalda, a human movement scientist at the University of Twente, has some concerns about the impact of more ebike use, particularly if children lose a low-impact exercise that was once built into everyday life.

“Our whole infrastructure was built around bikes, so children bike to school, they bike to sports, they bike to all kinds of social activities,” he said. “It was always very easy for Dutch children to reach the norms of active, minimally active behaviour. If children are switching to ebikes, and that’s the trend, it is more challenging to reach the minimum number of active minutes to stay healthy.”

However, some experts warn it is easy to stereotype certain groups – such as “fatbike” users – for causing the tensions. Clara Glachant, a researcher in micromobility at Eindhoven University of Technology, said electric bikes could have a positive role in “expanding cycling to groups that do not cycle”.

Meredith Glaser, the chief executive of the Urban Cycling Institute in Amsterdam, said four in 10 cyclists who died in recent years were in a collision with a car. “Any pointing of fingers towards cyclists is an excellent scapegoat for the uncomfortable reality that cars and trucks are still taking up the majority of public space and causing the most harm to the environment and to human bodies,” she said.

articles.summary: A Human Rights Watch report found that Modi's rule in India has eroded the rule of law and "systematically weakened institutions" meant to protect freedoms. Also, in Delhi a man injured nine police…

image.caption: PM Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party has often faced allegations of weaponizing federal agencies and eroding human rights, especially of minoritiesImage: Idrees Mohammed/AFP

blocks.text: Live

A Human Rights Watch report found that Modi's rule in India has eroded the rule of law and "systematically weakened institutions" meant to protect freedoms. Also, in Delhi a man injured nine police with a knife.
Prefer DW on Google

blocks.caption: PM Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party has often faced allegations of weaponizing federal agencies and eroding human rights, especially of minoritiesImage: Idrees Mohammed/AFP

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Report warns against India's democratic backsliding under Prime Minister Narendra Modi
Man injures nine police officer with knife, held after several gunshots

blocks.text: Here are the biggest headlines from India on Tuesday, November 24:
November 24, 2026
India deepens authoritarian slide under Modi — Report

blocks.caption: Modi has spent over 12 years as India's premierImage: Seshadri Sukumar/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Modi's Hindu nationalist government has "systematically weakened" institutions meant to protect human rights and democratic freedoms, a scathing new report by Human Rights Watch concluded.

In a 95-page report titled 'So What's This Democracy We're Talking About?: Modi's Authoritarian Playbook in India,' the watchdog found that the right-wing Bharatiya Janata Party-led (BJP) government is undermining parliamentary procedures, suppressing opposition and weaponzing investigative agencies for political ends.
It also found that the government has weakened constitutional and statutory bodies meant to protect democratic freedoms and the rights of the people.
India's 'Cockroach' protesters claim online censorship
'Authoritarian playbook'

"Over the past decade, the Modi government has been hollowing out India’s independent institutions that are critical to checking executive power and protecting civil liberties," said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.

"The government has eroded the rule of law and promoted Hindu majoritarianism, rolling back human rights protections, undermining the rights of marginalized communities, and deepening India's authoritarian slide."

The report further claimed the Election Commission of India and the Supreme Court — both independent bodies — failed to uphold fundamental freedoms, pointing to the elimination of millions of voter names from India's electoral rolls in a controversial exercise.

blocks.caption: Nationwide protests against deleted voter names broke out in India in October, only to be met with widespread detentionsImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: "The Modi administration's actions over the past decade are not isolated institutional failures but mutually reinforcing elements of an authoritarian playbook," Human Rights Watch said.
"India's allies should press the Modi government to end its assault on independent institutions and restore checks on executive power," Pearson said.

The Bureau of Immigration (BI) deported 139 Indonesian fugitives on Tuesday, citing threats they posed to national security and public interest.
In a press release, the BI said the deportees were scheduled to leave the country aboard a chartered flight from the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) Terminal 3.
The group consisted of 111 men and 28 women who had previously been held in the custody of the Philippine National Police (PNP).

“The deportees ... were identified as fugitives by Indonesian authorities and subsequently classified as undesirable aliens under Philippine immigration laws for posing threats to national security and public interest,” the BI said.
The BI Board of Commissioners issued a Summary Deportation Order against the group on Nov. 19.
The order was implemented through coordination among the BI, the PNP Aviation Security Group and the Indonesian Embassy.
BI Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado said the bureau would continue expediting the deportation of foreign fugitives to protect the country's security and public interest.

articles.title: South Korea tells island residents to take shelter after Russian military aircraft approach
articles.summary:
The order was issued after aircraft entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the island of Ulleungdo

Residents of a remote South Korean island were ordered to take shelter…

blocks.text: Residents of a remote South Korean island were ordered to take shelter on Tuesday morning after several Russian military aircraft came close to entering its airspace, prompting a pre-emptive alert from the military that anticipated a violation.
The defence ministry said it would summon the Russian defence attaché on Tuesday afternoon to lodge a strong protest.

The joint chiefs of staff (JCS) said the aircraft had entered the country’s air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan – known in South Korea as the East Sea – and approached the island of Ulleungdo. It did not specify how many Russian aircraft were involved, but South Korean air force jets were scrambled before the aircraft left.

A JCS spokesperson, Jang Do-young, said the aircraft had approached “to the point just before violating Ulleungdo’s airspace” and that, because military aircraft move very fast, a violation was anticipated.
The alert was issued pre-emptively to protect residents, he said.

The interior ministry issued the emergency alert at 7.52am to residents of Ulleungdo, a volcanic island of about 8,700 people 120km off the east coast, telling them to take shelter. The English portion of the message read: “EVACUATION, AIR RAID”.

Television broadcasts were interrupted by on-screen warnings telling residents to “prepare to evacuate to a nearby underground shelter facility and listen to broadcasting”. The alert was lifted at 7.55am.

On the island, sirens sounded and residents reportedly heard the noise of fighter jets. Jeong Hae-seung, 41, who was working on a building site, told the Hankyoreh newspaper he ran out of his workplace the moment the text arrived.

blocks.caption: A man jogs past a lighthouse at Jeodong port on the island of Ulleungdo. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I went outside wondering what on earth was going on, and the civil defence broadcast was playing, but I couldn’t make out what it was saying,” he said.
Baek Un-bae, who lives on the island, told broadcaster YTN that an elderly resident had telephoned him asking whether war had broken out.
“Older people have no access to the media, so all they hear is the warning broadcast and they are too alarmed to know what to do,” he said.
Others said they did not hear the sirens at all, with windows shut against the cold and strong winds blowing.
A second message, sent by North Gyeongsang province, which administers Ulleungdo, said a flying object “presumed to be a North Korean aircraft” had left the danger zone.
The province said it had mistakenly taken the wording from its routine drill messages, changed only the time and sent it in error.
Jang described the alert as unusual but said he could not confirm whether it was the first of its kind.
Tuesday’s incident was the fourth known entry by Russian military aircraft into the zone this year and the second in a week.

An air defence identification zone is not sovereign airspace, but countries establish such zones beyond their own airspace to identify incoming military flights early. While submitting a flight plan in advance is international practice, entering an identification zone without prior notification does not in itself violate international law.
Russia argues that the Korean zone has no basis in international law and does not recognise Seoul’s authority over it, and has repeatedly flown into it without notice.
According to data submitted to parliament, about 60 Russian entries without prior notification were recorded in the five years to 2024, compared with about 430 by Chinese aircraft.

Seoul previously summoned Russia’s defence attaché in March 2025 after eight entries in 10 days. At the time, it was the first such summons since a Russian aircraft violated South Korean airspace in 2019 and South Korean jets fired warning shots.

articles.title: Steven Galloway asks judge to declare rape allegations false as defamation trial enters final submissions
articles.summary: Former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway is asking the presiding justice in his defamation trial to vindicate his reputation by making an explicit finding of "falsehood," which…

image.caption: Steven Galloway, back centre, is seen through a window as he leaves B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver, on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. The author alleges defamation against a former student with whom he had an extramarital affair, and three other defendants. (Darryl Dyck/THE CANADIAN PRESS)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway is asking the presiding justice in his defamation trial to vindicate his reputation by making an explicit finding of "falsehood," which would essentially clear the author of the rape and sexual assault accusation levelled against him over a decade ago.
Former UBC prof undeserving of 'horrific stain' on his name for more than decade, says lawyer
Former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway is asking the presiding justice in his defamation trial to vindicate his reputation by making an explicit finding of "falsehood."

"There's been a horrific stain on his name for over a decade," said Galloway's lead counsel Daniel Burnett during closing submissions on Monday. "It's in the public interest to have a final resolution of these allegations that have floated around for so long."
Galloway alleges defamation against a former student with whom he had an extramarital affair, and three other defendants who repeated rape allegations online and elsewhere.

items: Sexual assault claims 'flat out never happened,' ex-UBC professor tells defamation trial

blocks.text: Galloway's main accuser, identified only as A.B. because of a publication ban, earlier withdrew her defence of justification, choosing not to argue that claims Galloway raped or sexually assaulted her on three occasions in 2011 were true. Justice Neena Sharma had said the woman had not admitted that her accusations are false and the court couldn't make assumptions until it hears all evidence.

A.B. is a former UBC graduate student who is five years older than Galloway. She did not appear or testify at trial because of mental health concerns. Three other defendants — Mandi Gray, Glynnis Kirchmeier and Dana Kagis — are alleged to have repeated A.B.'s claims on social media and elsewhere.

"It's an unfortunate reality in this day and age that truth can often end up being in the hands of those who shout the loudest, those who tweet the most and those who recruit the most allies. And the court trial process is the last stop," Burnett told Sharma.
Steven Galloway is pictured in his office at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver on March 31, 2014. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
A.B. brought her allegations to UBC in November 2015. Soon after, Galloway was suspended, a move the university announced publicly by citing "serious allegations" against him.
A retired judge hired by UBC to conduct an investigation found that on a balance of probabilities he had not committed sexual assault.
Galloway was fired for misconduct. He was never criminally investigated.

items: UBC prof testifies she acted as a 'conduit' for sex assault allegations against Steven Galloway

blocks.text: Burnett told the court there was "overwhelming evidence of deliberate and calculated falsehoods built upon falsehoods." He said A.B. ran a strategic campaign to leverage criminal accusations against Galloway through other people.

That included, Burnett said, A.B. lying to friends and UBC officials that her story would be featured on an episode of the CBC's fifth estate if UBC didn't act against Galloway, and that CBC lawyers had found her evidence of the rape to be damning.

Burnett said A.B.'s "fabrications" cast serious doubt on everything she said, citing a disturbing claim A.B. made about being possibly drugged into unconsciousness and violently raped by Galloway in his UBC office.

Burnett said text messages between A.B. and her ex-husband on the night in question, along with other inconsistencies in her account, demonstrated that the allegation was not simply false but a "knowing lie."

items: Defendant apologizes to B.C. writer days before defamation trial to start

blocks.text: The author of The Cellist of Sarajevo admitted during testimony that he and A.B. had an affair between 2011 and 2013 while both were married.
His defamation lawsuit filed in 2018 originally named more than 20 defendants, the majority of whom settled before the trial began. A number of the defendants have also issued public apologies.
Burnett said Galloway has endured loss and suffering since 2015 that no person should wish on another.
"Hopefully, the outcome of this case will — as far as any court decision can — enable him to recover something back and have a better future," said Burnett.
Defence's closing submissions are expected to begin Tuesday in B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Karin Larsen is a former Olympian and award-winning sports broadcaster who covers news and sports for CBC Vancouver.
With files from The Canadian Press

articles.title: Manila court orders arrest of Atong Ang, ex-cop in missing sabungeros case
articles.summary: A Manila court has issued a warrant of arrest against fugitive tycoon Atong Ang and former police officer Ryan Jay Orapa.

blocks.text: November 24, 2026 | 10:48am

Businessman Charlie "Atong" Ang, accompanied by his lawyer Lorna Kapunan, files criminal charges before the Mandaluyong City Prosecutor's Office on July 3, 2025 against Julie "Dondon" Patidongan and Alan Bantiles for accusations related to the case of "missing sabungeros."
The STAR / Michael Varcas
MANILA, Philippines — A Manila court has issued a warrant of arrest against fugitive tycoon Atong Ang and former police officer Ryan Jay Orapa.

In a message to reporters on Tuesday, November 24, Department of Justice spokesperson Polo Martinez said that the Manila Regional Trial Court Branch 175 issued the arrest warrant against Ang and Orapa on October 30.
“In its Order, the court found sufficient evidence to establish probable cause to hold both accused for trial for the offenses charged,” Martinez said.
The charges against Ang and Orapa are kidnapping and serious illegal detention. The said charges are non-bailable.
This came after the Manila court granted the prosecution’s motion to amend the information in the Manila Arena case, after the prosecution panel found prima facie evidence to charge Ang and Orapa.
However, one of the accused successfully sought the inhibition of Branch 185’s presiding judge, prompting the re-raffling of the case to Branch 175, according to Martinez.

Ang’s camp also moved to defer arraignment and suspend proceedings pending its petition for review with the DOJ, with the court noting the motion while the parties await further action and the next hearing date.
Ang has been in hiding since January 2026, after courts in Laguna and Batangas issued arrest warrants against him in connection with the missing-sabungeros cases. He has not been arrested since then.
Ang denies all the allegations against him.

articles.title: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.summary:
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says

A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying…

blocks.text: A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.
The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.
The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.
The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
articles.summary: German media said Russia planned to launch a satellite with a nuclear warhead into space in coming weeks.

blocks.text: Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.

Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.

Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.

Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.

A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.

Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.

In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

articles.title: Duterte camp opposes closed-door testimonies for ICC witnesses
articles.summary: The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has opposed the International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution's request for several witnesses to testify behind closed doors, saying the sweeping…

blocks.text: November 24, 2026 | 10:09am

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has opposed the International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecution's request for several witnesses to testify behind closed doors, saying the sweeping use of such measures would undermine the public nature of the trial.

In an 11-page filing dated November 23, Duterte's counsel Peter Haynes and his team questioned the prosecution's request to keep most of its witnesses anonymous, saying it failed to establish that each witness faced an objectively justifiable risk.

The prosecution is seeking anonymity for 55 of its 69 witnesses, including 32 insiders. It also wants 22 witnesses to testify entirely in closed sessions, according to the defense's redacted submission.
"Simply put, the Prosecution is requesting anonymity for 79% of its testifying witnesses, 40% of whom would then give evidence effectively in secret," the defense said.

The defense argued that the extent of the requested measures would infringe on Duterte's right to a public trial, saying public scrutiny should not be a reason to keep testimonies away from public view.
"Contrary to the Prosecution's assertions, heightened public scrutiny and interest are not grounds to set aside the right to a public trial," the defense said.

"A public trial is, by its design, meant to ensure a fair trial, and foster trust and confidences in the genuine process of justice. That is not achieved when in-court evidence is given behind closed doors or by faceless witnesses with distorted voices," it added.

It also questioned the prosecution's basis for seeking witness protection, saying factors such as a witness' public profile, increased media exposure, membership in the Philippine National Police (PNP) or government, residence in the Philippines or familiarity with Duterte were insufficient grounds for granting protective measures.
The defense said the prosecution had failed to establish that the same objectively justifiable risks applied to each witness in the categories for which protection was being sought.
It also raised concerns over the extent of evidence that would be withheld from public view if the request were granted.

According to the filing, the prosecution is seeking to anonymize all in-court evidence involving 46 charged incidents, leaving identifiable evidence for only 10 incidents, and even then, only partially.

The defense said the proposed public testimony for nine of the 10 incidents would rely on four witnesses whose evidence was "confined to second hand information and/or the aftermaths of the alleged killings."
"Anonymising evidence so extensive yet so determinative of the case is incompatible with the principles of publicity and transparency in this trial," the defense said.

The defense maintained that it does not oppose private sessions when the prosecution can establish that witnesses face objectively justifiable risks and that their answers may reveal their identities.
However, it objected to the request to place 22 witnesses under entirely closed sessions, saying less restrictive measures could address the alleged risks.
The defense proposed the targeted use of private sessions, along with pseudonyms and face and voice distortions, instead of withholding entire testimonies from the public.
It also argued that witness anonymity could affect the ICC's ability to establish the truth, as public testimony allows people to scrutinize the credibility and reliability of witnesses.

"Public anonymity may affect the ability of the Chamber to fulfill its truth-seeking mandate, as making a witness's identity known to the public increases their commitment to tell the truth as well as their feeling of public accountability," the defense said.
It added that keeping allegations hidden would deprive the defense of information from the public that could help challenge witness accounts.
"If the allegations are all kept hidden from public view, the Defence loses one of the most important tools in its investigative arsenal; allegations being made in full view of the public," it said.
The defense also opposed the prosecution's request for special measures for an unnamed witness, saying there was no basis to consider the individual vulnerable.
"There is no reason to believe [REDACTED] is a vulnerable witness," the defense said.

In its concluding requests, the defense asked the ICC Trial Chamber III to consider the proportionate use of pseudonyms and face and voice distortions, reject requests for entirely closed sessions for certain witnesses, and decide on private sessions on a case-by-case basis.

The filing comes ahead of the scheduled opening of Duterte's ICC trial on November 30. He is facing three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder over killings allegedly committed in the Philippines between Nov. 1, 2011 and March 16, 2019, as part of his administration's war on drugs.

articles.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator asks court to revoke detention order
articles.summary: According to court filings, Melody Bryant was not the only one who initially failed to recognize killer Jesse Van Rootselaar was "genuinely dangerous." The motion says records show the shooter shared…

image.caption: Melody Bryant, who was charged under the name James Cody Bryant in October, is seen in a court sketch. The alleged co-conspirator of Tumbler Ridge school shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar has applied to revoke a U.S. detention order. (Lois Silver)

blocks.text: An American accused of helping Jesse Van Rootselaar plan the Tumbler Ridge massacre has filed an application to get out of jail, asking a Seattle court judge to review and revoke a previous detention order.

A magistrate judge ordered the detention of Melody Bryant, who was charged under the name James Cody Bryant in October, after the government argued the accused would be a danger to the public if released.
Bryant, 30, is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, an offence that carries a maximum sentence of life in prison and a $250,000 US fine. She has pleaded not guilty.
The trial was originally scheduled to begin next month, but has been moved to December 2027.

Her lawyers say in court filings that their client is not a danger to the public and should be released with conditions. They say at the time of the Oct. 13 detention hearing, they had not yet received discovery documents and could not properly respond to the government's argument.
U.S. resident allegedly gave advice, money to Tumbler Ridge shooter
On Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother Jennifer Strang, 39, and half-brother Emmett Jacobs, 11, in their home.

She then drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where she gunned down Abel Mwansa, 12, Zoey Benoit, 12, Ezekiel Schofield, 13, Kylie Smith, 12, Ticaria Lampert, 12, and educational assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39.
Two other students were shot but survived.

items: Alleged co-conspirator in Tumbler Ridge shooting has trial delayed until December 2027

blocks.text: In their 33-page motion for revocation of detention order filed last week, Bryant's lawyers say the case is based mainly on nearly 74,000 individual texts between Van Rootselaar and Bryant on messaging platform Discord, sent between Aug. 1 and Feb. 10, 2025.
Approximately two-thirds of those messages, numbering 47,750, are from Van Rootselaar to Bryant.
Bryant's lawyers say while some of their clients messages "may be tasteless and, in retrospect, were ill considered" they are protected by the First Amendment.

"For better or worse, the First Amendment also protects their debate about whether a school shooting or attack on a crowd would be more likely to make someone infamous, even if the government tries to recast that conversation as 'tactical advice,'" said the Nov. 18 motion filed by Bryant's lawyers.
Discord messages reveal Tumbler Ridge shooter, U.S. resident planning attack
The motion includes excerpts of chats between Bryant and Van Rootselaar, including one on Christmas Day 2025 used to show instances where Bryant refused to engage in violent rants.
"I hope I ruin everyone's life when I do my plan. I want nobody to recover … whenever I say some mentally ill ahh stuff I feel like u stop messaging me lol…," wrote Van Rootselaar.
Bryant wrote back, "Harder to reply to."
The court filings say, for part of the six-month period where Bryant spoke daily to Van Rootselaar, the shooter's "plan" was clearly a fantasy because Van Rootselaar did not have access to guns.
"Eventually, however, the RCMP returned her seized weapons."
Seized guns used in shooting: documents

According to the court filings, Bryant was not the only one who initially failed to recognize Van Rootselaar was "genuinely dangerous." The motion says records show the shooter shared her plans widely and had even "received encouragement from other online contacts."
She got tactical advice from ChatGPT, family and friends bought her ammunition, even after she was released from psychiatric hospitalization and the RCMP, according to the motion.

items: Tumbler Ridge shooter stole guns from family safe as part of attack plans, new court filings reveal
RCMP says it still won't share more details on firearms used in Tumbler Ridge shooting

blocks.text: Bryant's lawyers add that the RCMP had removed, and then later returned, Van Rootselaar's guns, "one of which had been altered to enable more rapid firing."
"In fact, the RCMP apparently returned the gun with the alteration intact. Van Rootselaar then used the altered firearm in the shooting," said the Nov. 18 motion.

Days after the Tumbler Ridge shooting, RCMP said a long gun and modified rifle were seized from the school, and two firearms including a shotgun were seized among a number of other firearms at the residence.

The shotgun is believed to have been used in the homicides at the home and had not been previously seized by police. Mounties also said they had not previously seized the main firearm used in the school shooting and its origins are unknown.
Report details Tumbler Ridge shooter’s alleged ChatGPT interactions
Bryant's lawyers say their client promised not to snitch on the shooter because Bryant believed it would result in violence, and accelerate the shooter's homicidal plans.

"While it is horrifying in retrospect to imagine that Ms. Bryant might have stopped Van Rootselaar from committing a terrible crime if she had contacted the police, it is undisputed that the law provided no affirmative duty to do so," said the motion.
The court filings said in the past Bryant was able to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing a crime, and did not understand violence was imminent.
A memorial for the victims of a school shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School is pictured on Feb. 11, 2026. (Ben Nelms/CBC)
Bryant's lawyers say the shooter viewed Bryant as "a nonjudgemental sounding board for ruminating about her mental illness," and that Bryant helped her resist her urges.
The defence included chats to illustrate that.
In an undated message, Van Rootselaar writes "I **really** wanna shoot ppl, idk what to do with that feeling lmao. Like how do I relieve that? I can't talk about it much even."
"Yeah I think most would snitch," replies Bryant.
"Except for you who silently discourage it and a few others who openly encourage it," responds Van Rootselaar.
Government distorted evidence: defence

Bryant's lawyers say the U.S. government's 41-page complaint against their client is "replete with distortions" and includes rearranged text messages made to appear that Bryant was agreeing to help the shooter build a bomb.

The motion for revocation of detention order says the conversation included in the complaint showing Bryant agreeing to pay for a lighter needed to make a bomb occurred over two days and in between 225 messages.

"In fact, nowhere in the complete chats does Van Rootselaar say that she needs a lighter for the bomb. Nowhere does Bryant offer to provide Van Rootselaar a lighter for that purpose," said the court filing.
U.S. resident met Tumbler Ridge shooter on Omegle: FBI
Bryant's lawyers say the decision to piece the texts together "seems designed to lead the magistrate judge to make a false inference."
They say while Bryant agreed to watch a livestream and if possible distribute it, she did not agree with Van Rootselaar's plans to kill people.
The motion says the fact that law enforcement left Bryant in the community for seven months after reviewing her Discord chats shows she does not pose a danger.
The magistrate judge concluded Bryant suffers from a "deeply rooted" mental illness and substance abuse history.

Bryant's lawyers say that is not true. Bryant is currently being treated for gender dysphoria and had previously been prescribed medication for anxiety but no longer takes that drug, according to the motion.
The U.S. state's attorney's response is due Wednesday, then a judge will decide if Bryant should be released.

articles.title: How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
articles.summary: BBC's Lily Jamali reports from Nvidia's headquarters, where she gauges the reaction to Huang's return after Trump says he brokered a deal.

blocks.text: Nvidia's board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO and president on Monday. President Trump has claimed credit for brokering the deal. What is the mood at Nvidia following the announcement? BBC's Lily Jamali reports from Nvidia's headquarters, where she gauges the reaction to Huang's return.
Video edited by Mabel Pickering

articles.title: Nvidia reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after affair with alleged spy as Trump says 'I made the deal'
articles.summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.

blocks.text: The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.
Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".
"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.
Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," Republican congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska said.
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."
Sen Tom Cotton, fellow Republican who represents Arkansas, vowed that Congress would investigate.
"The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back," he said.
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress from January, have already promised to launch Nvidia investigations.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".

Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a member of the House foreign affairs committee, also condemned the move in a statement to the BBC as "premature" before multiple investigations are concluded. Fellow Democratic Representative Andre Carson, a member of the House intelligence committee, told the BBC that "Congress needs a full accounting of whether any controlled technology was diverted" to China.
Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December.
Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.

Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.

A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.
The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.
Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
The BBC has contacted the White House.

Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.
The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.
With additional reporting from Brandon Drenon and Rachel Clun

articles.title: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend Molly Meldrum
articles.summary: The promoter and broadcaster helped define the music tastes of Australians for decades.

blocks.text: King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.
Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.
The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.
Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.
Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.
Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.
"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.
Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.
He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".
On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."
Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.
"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."
"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

articles.title: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police
articles.summary: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
articles.byline: Nomsa Maseko, Thuthuka Zondi, Eleanor Smallwood

blocks.text: Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student
ByNomsa MasekoThuthuka Zondi and Eleanor Smallwood BBC World ServiceReporting fromEkurhuleni
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.
It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.
"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.
But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.
When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.
"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

blocks.text: Image source, Thuthuka Zondi/BBC
Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death
Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.
She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.
Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.
It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.
South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.
Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa
The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confront widespread violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.
But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.
For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.
Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.
"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.
The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa
According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.
This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".
Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.
Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.
"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

blocks.text: Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00
Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.
Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.
In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.
Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.
The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.
Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.
Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.
"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."
Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

blocks.text: Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her
Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.
She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.
When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.
"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.
She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.
Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.
In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.
She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.
Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

blocks.text: Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles
In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.
She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.
Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.
"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

blocks.text: Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed
Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.
Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.
Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.
Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

articles.title: 'I'm not a hero,' says Arizona man who found lost toddler alone in the desert
articles.summary: Search parties with helicopters, K-9 units and heat-seeking drones scoured the rural dessert community of Eloy, Ariz. for hours looking two-year-old Vella Campillo after she wandered away from her…

image.caption: Body cam footage shows the moment police arrived on the scene after Arizona resident Jay Stewart found missing toddler Vella Campillo hiding in a bush in the desert earlier this month. (Pinal County Sheriff's Office)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

Search parties with helicopters, K-9 units and heat-seeking drones scoured the rural dessert community of Eloy, Ariz. for hours looking two-year-old Vella Campillo after she wandered away from her backyard — all to no avail. Then Jay Stewart found her hiding in a bush.
Police, dogs and drones scoured area for 2-year-old to no avail. Then Jay Stewart found her in a bush
Jay Stewart has a lot of precious memories, but he says nothing compares to the moment he found two-year-old Vella Campillo alone in the cold, dark Arizona desert, wearing nothing but a diaper.

Police are hailing Stewart as a hero after he found the missing toddler who wandered away from her backyard last week, sparking a massive search-and-rescue operation in the rural community of Eloy, Ariz.
"I am so grateful to have experienced that life event, because there's no other feeling like it in the world," Stewart told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
"That's No. 1 in my life, the most emotional moment I've ever had."
Vella was unharmed and has been safely reunited with her parents, police said.
LISTEN | Interview with Jay Stewart about finding Vella:
As It Happens6:16Arizona man describes the emotional moment he found a lost toddler alone in the desert
Vella was reported missing around 6 p.m., local time, on Nov. 17, according to the Pinal County Sheriff's Office.
Her parents, Joseph Campillo and Deanna Fritz, told Fox News affiliate KSAZ that she'd been playing in the backyard with her siblings under the care of another family member when she wandered off.
Officials from several police and fire departments spent hours scouring the area along with dozens of volunteers, two helicopters, K-9 units and heat-detecting drones, all to no avail.
Then, just after midnight, Stewart called Vella's name and saw her pop out of a tiny patch of plants in the desert.

"I spun around, and she jumped back down into this little bush … the size of, like, four dinner plates put together," he said. "She almost looked like she was swimming. Her little arms were moving around like she was treading water."
Pitch black and freezing cold
Stewart and his wife had been looking for Vella ever since the emergency alert hit their phones notifying people of a missing child in their area.
They spent two hours searching along the side of the road, he says, before heading home to check the news and bundle up in warmer clothes as the sun went down and the cold set in.
"The desert is kind of like being in a mine. It could be pitch black where you can't see anything. And that's what it was like," he said.
On their second try, they drove into the desert behind Vella's home on their ATV.
"I've lived out there 20 years and I fly over it all the time in our helicopter. So I know it like the back of my hand," he said. "It's my backyard."
Pinal County Sheriff Ross Teeple, right, awarded Stewart a plaque and a badge the day after he found a missing toddler near Eloy, Ariz. (Pinal County Sheriff’s Office)
Stewart says he'd separated from his wife as he wandered about a mile down a ditch calling Vella's name. He heard a yell, then saw her pop up and back down again.
He reached down, plucked her into his arms, unzipped his jacket and tucked her inside.
"She whimpered for about 15 seconds when I picked her up, and then once I snuggled her to me and got her, she seemed pretty happy," he said. "She warmed up pretty quick."
Stewart says she didn't make a peep until he dropped his phone while talking to a 911 dispatcher.
"And she went, 'Phone!' I started laughing. And I'm like, 'Yeah, baby, phone!' " he said. "It chokes me up. I can hear that little voice."

items: Indiana woman crashes car into ditch, survives on creek water for 6 days
This 77-year-old spent a night alone on a mountain. He raised over $30K for his rescuers

blocks.text: Within 10 minutes, he says, police and other searchers were on the scene.

Body cam footage released by the Pinal County Sheriff's Office shows Stewart holding the toddler on his hip. By that point, she was wrapped in a blanket provided by another searcher and chattering away happily in baby talk.
When the officer took Vella to check her over, the little girl clutched onto Stewart.
"She wouldn't let go of me," he said.
'The very best of our community'
At a news conference on Nov. 18, Sheriff Ross Teeple awarded Stewart a plaque and a badge for his community service.

"Your selflessness and willingness to get involved amplify the very best of our community," Teeple said. "Your actions remind us that every citizen has the power to make a meaningful difference and that sometimes, the greatest acts of service come from simply choosing to help."
But Stewart says he was just one of dozens of volunteers who showed up for Vella, and he happened to get lucky.
"I'm not a hero. I'm a searcher, just like everyone else was," he said.
He called the rescue the most emotional moment of his life, followed by the birth of his children and the day he married his wife.

"The reason I put it ahead of my kids is because I knew where my kids were. They weren't lost. I was holding them," he said. "But to find something that's lost like that, helpless and lost? I can only imagine what the parents were going through."
Interview with Jay Stewart produced by Chris Trowbridge

articles.title: Rights group details 'surge' in violent attacks on Palestinian health-care workers
articles.summary: Based on testimony from health-care workers, Physicians for Human Rights Israel says there’s been a 350 per cent increase in violence against Palestinian health workers by settlers and the Israeli…

image.caption: Palestinian men inspect torched vehicles following a rampage by Israeli settlers east of Ramallah, where Yousef Dihir works as a paramedic. (Mahmoud Illean/AP Photo)

blocks.text: World·New

Based on testimony from health-care workers, Physicians for Human Rights Israel says there’s been a 350 per cent increase in violence against Palestinian health workers by settlers and the Israeli military. Israel denies the report's claims.
Violence jumped 350% from 2022-2024, Physicians for Human Rights Israel says
For Yousef Dihir, a paramedic since 2008 in the West Bank, treating his fellow Palestinians has become a daily — sometimes lethal — risk.

Leaning against his ambulance in Ramallah, Palestine, earlier this month, he told CBC News about one of the many incidents of settler violence he's faced after receiving a distress call. On this particular occasion, three years ago, his son had come along as a volunteer paramedic.
"My son was injured, we were hit with glass in our faces when the gunshots broke out on the ambulance," he said. "They shot at the rear glass and the front glass."

In a report published this week, Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) says settler violence affecting health-care workers "surged 350 per cent" between 2022 and 2024 in the West Bank, from 93 violent encounters to 422.
Attacks on Palestinian medics in West Bank surge 350%: rights group

PHRI documented instances of violence against health-care workers through interviews with 25 paramedics, medics and emergency response workers, Dihir included, as well by accompanying paramedics and ambulance drivers during their shifts to see first-hand how they navigated checkpoints to get to patients.

PHRI says the uptick in violence has been particularly notable since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins and its two million people living in dire conditions.
Since then, PHRI says, "restrictions on medical care under the violent occupation have increasingly given way to direct attacks by Israeli forces and settlers on emergency medical services."
They say it's clear that the health-care workers were targeted in particular through "broader policies sustaining Israel's unlawful occupation of the West Bank."

items: Gaza is slowly moving beyond survival mode — 3 years after the war began
UN commission says Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza since truce

blocks.text: The number of obstacles blocking movement around the West Bank has also increased, from 642 in June 2023 to 925 in December 2025.
"Reaching patients, evacuating the wounded and transferring patients between medical facilities all depend on Israeli military approval," the report says.
"Interviewees describe physical assaults, threats at gunpoint, verbal abuse, humiliating searches and being prevented from reaching wounded or seriously ill patients."
The report notes an uptick in violent altercations between settlers and paramedics in the West Bank since Oct. 7, 2023. (Bashar Qaryuti/PHRI)

In 2025, the World Health Organization recorded a total of 233 attacks on health-care workers in the West Bank. And 38 attacks were recorded between January and April 2026, "35 of which involved obstruction of health care."
It is a violation of international law, said Milena Ansari, director of the Occupied West Bank at PHRI, at a news conference on Nov. 16.

Citing the Fourth Geneva Convention, which guarantees protection of civilians during armed conflict, Ansari said Israel has a responsibility to ensure medical services and public health access to "the occupied population."
"And this explicitly extends to Palestinian paramedics, ambulances and emergency medical teams."

items: Israeli settler violence at unprecedented levels during Palestinian olive harvest

blocks.text: IDF denies claims, condemns 'acts of violence'

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) denied claims that their security forces were stopping medical teams from doing their work and "condemned all acts of violence against medical teams and ambulances," in a statement to CBC News.
"The IDF enables freedom of movement for medical teams through Judea and Samaria and coordinates the movement of Palestinian ambulances with relevant authorities in advance," the statement says.
Ansari said that's not enough.

items: Israeli settler violence at unprecedented levels during Palestinian olive harvest
Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including surgeon, health authorities say

blocks.text: "We should be setting a high standard of removing all checkpoints, removing all barriers that are between Palestinian communities and Palestinian territories," she said.

In one case, a paramedic described being kept away from an injured man. "I was standing close to the wounded man. I could have reached him easily, but the soldiers stopped me. He lay there bleeding until he died. Only then did they leave, and we were able to reach him," the paramedic recounted to PHRI.

The United Nations Office for Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the highest number of violent attacks in the West Bank has been recorded in 2026 to date with over 2,000 attacks against Palestinians resulting in death or property damage.
Paramedics 'constantly on edge,' report says
PHRI is calling on Israel to end all violence against medical workers in the West Bank and ensure the unhindered passage of ambulances through checkpoints, gates and closed areas.
They are also calling on the government to investigate settler violence and prosecute all attacks against medical workers.
Multiple countries urge Israel to allow aid into Gaza
The PHRI report also documents the "severe psychological toll on emergency workers," with many noting feelings of distress, anxiety and sleep disturbances.
"All 25 described being constantly on edge, fearing they could be stopped, attacked or prevented from reaching patients," it says.
Dihir said one of his colleagues died in April 2023 during an altercation with settlers.
"He was shot in the head but he refused to stop," he said. "He was afraid for the lives of the injured." His patients survived the attack.
While Dihir admits he doesn't want to die, he says he's not scared.
"I don't care about religion, race, ethnicity or anything else. ... I only care that a person needs humanitarian help and I can do that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Yasmine Hassan is a producer in CBC's Ottawa bureau. From there, she covers developments inside Gaza and the West Bank related to the Israel-Hamas war. If you have a story idea, send news tips in English or Arabic to yasmine.hassan@cbc.ca.
