articles.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
articles.summary:
Carney watches on as comedian lampoons US leader and his interest in men’s backsides at correspondents’ event Ottawa

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a…

blocks.text: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.

With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.

He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”

He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.

“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.

“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”

He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.

The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

articles.title: US adds Megaspeed, at center of Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist
articles.summary: The Trump administration has added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist after tensions over its failure to do so raised questions. The news came the same day that Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's…

image.caption: The firm was suspected of helping Nvidia chips reach China despite US export restrictions [PHOTO: November 10, 2026]Image: Taryn Ng/AFP

blocks.text: The Trump administration added Megaspeed International, the firm at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, to a trade blacklist on Monday.
That means that the Singapore-based firm will not be able to obtain US technology, including semiconductors, without obtaining a license from the US government.
The news was reported by Semafor, an American news website.
US Commerce Department under scrutiny over Nvidia scandal: What to know
The US Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed was smuggling Nvidia chips into China for more than a year, according to the Financial Times.
But tensions at the Commerce Department broke into the spotlight after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with an executive at the Singapore-based firm earlier this month.

Politicians criticized Commerce Department Secretary Howard Lutnick for not having previously added Megaspeed to the department's so-called "Entity List" despite US intelligence warnings that the company was a possible front for smuggling sensitive AI chip technology to China.
Huang briefly lost his job over the scandal as US officials said the woman, Alice Huang, was a Chinese spy.

blocks.caption: Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang in Taipei in 2025 Image: TVBS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday, in a stunning reversal after his resignation just two weeks ago.

The New York Times reported last month that US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset who passed information to Beijing while developing a close relationship with Jensen Huang.
Beijing has denied those claims and called the spy accusations "groundless."
Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
Nvidia shares soared more than 30% after the company announced it reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
Some people were happy to see him back as president of Nvidia, as videos posted to social media show.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is on track to be the next speaker of the House, called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible, and incomprehensible" and vowed Congress would reinvestigate any wrongdoing by the company and the Commerce Department.

articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
articles.summary: The publisher of an essay on coercive control apologises for "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

blocks.text: Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.
The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.
The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."
"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.
The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.
French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.
In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.
"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.
Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.
French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".
"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.
Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".
Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.
Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.
Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

articles.title: Girl, 14, planned random killing of child at her former Winnipeg elementary school: Crown
articles.summary: A teen girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the…

image.caption: A Winnipeg teen who allegedly plotted to kill a kindergarten-aged child at random was granted bail by a judge Thursday. (Martin Diotte/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·New

A teen girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the teen was granted bail last week.
Teen radicalized online by 'nihilistic, violent extremism culture,' expert testifies
WARNING: This story contains references to extreme violence involving children, and teen suicide.

A 14-year-old girl accused of planning to kill a child at her former Winnipeg elementary school was radicalized online and had a romantic fantasy about an American school shooter, a court heard before the teen was granted bail last week.

The girl, who cannot be identified under the Youth Criminal Justice Act, was granted bail by provincial court Judge Lindy Choy in a Winnipeg courtroom Thursday, according to recordings reviewed by CBC News. The teen is charged with one count of uttering threats.

She was admitted to a psychiatric unit for children and youth twice since July, with the most recent instance coming after her parents found written plans to kill a kindergarten-aged child at her former elementary school in early September, Crown prosecutor Jennifer Comack said.
The girl later expressed disbelief at her release from that facility, writing she had "fool[ed] everybody," Comack said.
"I have no idea how I got away with this with no legal consequences," the girl wrote in a journal seized by police on Oct. 15, according to the prosecutor.
"I told them it was just a joke and a hypothetical and they just ... believed it??? I mean, good for me."

Comack said the girl first gained police attention in July, when she was 13, after she tried to board a flight from Winnipeg to Toronto using credit card information she secretly obtained from her parents.

She planned to take a bus to Niagara Falls and walk across the Canada-U.S. border, where an 18-year-old man would have picked her up, Comack said. The girl later told her parents she was heading there to "participate in a suicide pact," Comack said.

items: Parents warned extremist groups are targeting a growing number of kids online across Prairies

blocks.text: The teen was initially admitted to the psychiatric unit after the July incident, but there was a "deep escalation" and "key shift" in her behaviour upon her release, as she began to engage with "nihilistic, violent extremism culture," Comack said.

Const. Andrea Lefort, a terrorism and extremism specialist with the Winnipeg Police Service, testified on Nov. 16 that the girl was radicalized online and is a "classic" example of young people who engage with "some of the most horrific" online content involving extreme violence and gore.

Lefort said the girl engaged with online communities that seek to emulate and "almost" fantasize about previous school attackers and mass killers, particularly Dylan Klebold — one of two teen gunmen who massacred 12 students and a teacher before killing themselves at Columbine High School in Colorado in 1999.
"We do see that with this online community, where in some cases, they will not just emulate them and want to mimic them, hence them planning their attacks," the constable said.

"But, in some cases, we will see a fantasy romance. And we do see that as well with [her], where we see her talking about her love for Dylan, and even talking about maybe seeing him at some point in the future, even though he's long since deceased."
The case represents "uncharted waters" for the Winnipeg Police Service, Lefort said.
'We are scared,' mother tells judge

The girl wrote about going to her former elementary school under the guise of visiting old teachers, hiding in the washroom and killing any child who entered, then "parad[ing] the corpse around the school to terrorize the children, before fleeing and killing herself," Comack said.
"What's the fun in killing yourself if you don't take anyone down with you?" the girl wrote, according to Comack.
She also wrote about the challenge in deciding what weapon to use, the prosecutor said.

"If I was in the [United] States, this would be an easy choice — a gun, duh — but I'm in Canada, which makes this a lot harder," she wrote. "I could use a hammer since the target would be a small child, maybe a knife. I think I'll bring both."

items: An extremist group has been linked to a Winnipeg terrorism-related case. What is M.K.Y.?

blocks.text: In another entry, the girl said she set the attack for Nov. 2, calling it "doom hour."
"Yay!!! It's nice having an official date."

Police and the former school were alerted about the planned attack in early October, court heard. The girl was arrested as she was discharged from the psychiatric facility on Oct. 15, which is when she gave a statement to police.
The girl told police she'd had unrestricted Internet access since age seven, and watched "cartel Mexican death videos as early as that age," Comack said.
"It is chilling to watch her, in her police statement, talk so matter of fact about killing a child," the prosecutor said.

As Lefort spoke about some extreme online communities' glorification of mass killers and their lack of empathy for the victims, someone on a court recording is heard saying, "So, just for the record, she is smiling right now."
The judge later asked the teen why she was smiling.
"It's awkward," the girl replied. "It's not smiling about the case or situation, it's more so just awkward."
The girl said she wanted to "get better," as she'd recently experienced "some really insane episodes," she said.

items: Violent extremism targeting kids online an 'escalating threat': Winnipeg police

blocks.text: "Sometimes, I just get really angry about something ... stupid."
The girl's mother, who was in the courtroom alongside her father, said they love and support their daughter but, "we are scared."
Comack said the Crown didn't oppose the girl's release but wanted to ensure she'll have no access to the Internet unless supervised by someone pre-approved.

The girl agreed to that condition, as well as staying away from her former elementary school, which CBC News is not naming to protect the girl's identity as required by the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

articles.title: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
articles.summary: The UK is joined by several other nations in recognising an ICJ ruling that Myanmar carried out genocide.

blocks.text: The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.

Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing, who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.
He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."

Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".
The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.
He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.

The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention, external.

In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.
Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi, was deposed by the military in 2021.
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.

articles.title: Iranian singer and four others receive lashes after performance without hijab
articles.summary:
Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law

An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each…

blocks.text: An Iranian singer and four members of her production team ⁠have each received 74 lashes after being sentenced for “offending public decency by producing and ⁠publishing obscene and ⁠immoral ​content online”, an Iranian news website said on Monday.
Parastoo Ahmadi and the four ⁠others were also handed two-year bans on artistic and musical activities and travel, the Emtedad website ⁠quoted lawyer Mostafa Nili as saying.

The case followed the ​release of a ‌video on YouTube ‌in December 2024 showing Ahmadi performing without the mandatory hijab alongside ‌male musicians in Qom, south of the capital Tehran, Norway-based human rights group Hengaw said.

Western governments and human rights groups have criticised flogging as torture and a violation of international law. Iran rejects accusations over ‌its human rights record, saying western countries should focus on their own human rights ​problems.

Rules requiring women to wear the hijab were a flashpoint during protests in 2022 after the ⁠death in custody of Kurdish Iranian woman Mahsa Amini, ​who was ​arrested for allegedly violating ​the dress code.
The rules have increasingly been ​flouted on ‌the streets of Tehran ​and ​beyond, and enforcement of the rules has also become more selective.

articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.summary: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.

blocks.text: Anchored up in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

articles.title: Denmark: Top court backs hardline immigration "ghetto law"
articles.summary: Denmark's Supreme Court has found that evictions of "non-Western" residents do not amount to discrimination. The government in Copenhagen argues its "ghetto law" encourages integration.

image.caption: At least 60% of social housing units must be let to 'Westerners' by 2030 according to Danish lawImage: Liselotte Sabroe/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP

blocks.text: Denmark's Supreme Court on Monday ruled in favor of a housing association that terminated 91 leases in order to prevent the label "hard ghetto" being applied to their housing complex. The decision align's with Copenhagen's hardline approach to immigration.

The court on Monday upheld Denmark's 2018 "ghetto law," which allows for the relocation of "non-Western" residents from minority-heavy neighborhoods in order to foster integration. The Danish court ruling diverges from a top EU court decision last year that found application of the law could amount to discrimination.

The Danish laws requires social housing estates to rebuild, renovate and adjust their social mix if these become minority heavy, stipulating that 60% of apartments be rented to "Westerners" at market value by 2030.
Denmark: Forcibly resettling 'ghettos'
Denmark's hardline immigration policies making it a role model in the EU

Denmark's pioneering role in spearheading tougher immigration rules has made it a model for some in the EU. Denmark was also one of five countries that last week announced its intent to set up an asylum seeker deportation hub in Rwanda.
Danish Housing Minister Jacob Mark welcomed Monday's decision, saying it "strengthens security, social cohesion and integration."
The court's decision upheld a 2022 lower court ruling against seven tenants who fought their evictions in Nojsomhed, Helsingor, just north of Copenhagen.

In Monday's ruling, the law was found to be non-discriminatory when it comes to the eviction of "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries" as it is not broadly based on ethnicity. The EU ruling focused on this particular aspect, saying the law would be discriminatory if criteria were race based, while ultimately allowing national courts to have the last say in the matter.

"The Supreme Court notes that applying the criterion of the law involves dividing people into two groups [immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries, and all other persons]. Both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups," read the Danish court's ruling.
What is the EU-Rwanda return hub scheme?
Who is a 'non-Western' resident?
Tenants' associations estimate that 11,000 people across Denmark will have to be relocated to comply with the law.

The housing association in question issued a written statement saying that it was aware that the evictions would impact those affected, adding that it undertook measures to insure that residents found new homes.

According to Statistics Denmark's definition, "non-Western" countries include every country other than the 27 member states of the European Union, as well as Andorra, Australia, Britain, Canada, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, New Zealand, Northern Ireland, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the United States and the Vatican.
Europe's asylum system is 'broken': Denmark's Stoklund

blocks.caption: Tess Ikonomou

blocks.text: Tess Ikonomou
Coalition objects to security agreement with Vanuatu
The Coalition has come out against a security agreement with Vanuatu because of objections to “binding conditions relating to the achievement of renewable energy and climate targets”.
In June, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and his Vanuatu counterpart, Jotham Napat, signed the Nakamal agreement in Canberra that rules out the use of its territory for foreign military bases.
Under the $500mn deal, Vanuatu stated it would “not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military base or infrastructure”.
But in dissenting comments released last night, Coalition members of a parliamentary committee scrutinising treaties said they did not support ratifying the agreement in its current form.

double quotation markWe acknowledge the legitimate concerns Vanuatu and other Pacific Island nations have regarding climate change and its impacts on their communities, economies, and national security. However, Coalition members object to clauses … that limit the ability of future governments to change current climate and energy policy settings, by creating binding conditions relating to the achievement of renewable energy and climate targets.
The Albanese government has forged a number of agreements, including new alliances with Fiji and Papua New Guinea, to deny China a military foothold in the Pacific.
A government spokesperson said the Coalition was “putting culture wars ahead of regional security. It is remarkable that the Liberals and Nationals continue to disrespect Pacific priorities.”
Penny Wong to defend US alliance
Penny Wong says abandoning the US would “surrender a central source of Australian strategic weight” at the moment the nation needs every tool available during global turmoil.
In a major foreign policy speech on Tuesday, the foreign affairs minister will take aim at opponents of the US alliance who present a retreat from the mutual defence pact as a “road to autonomy”.

double quotation markSuch a policy would surrender a central source of Australian strategic weight at precisely the moment we need every opportunity for influence available to us. What they would do is give us fewer choices and leave us more vulnerable, reducing our capacity to contribute to a regional balance in which our sovereignty can be protected.

The Greens are opposed to the Aukus security pact, under which Australia is set to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, in addition to the presence of the joint Pine Gap base in the Northern Territory.
Wong will also elevate artificial intelligence as a foreign policy challenge, warning the emerging technology is reordering lives, economies and militaries in ways not yet foreseen.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Israel seeks to jail Palestinian student activist without trial after dorm arrest
articles.summary:
Mahdi Tounsi appeared with visible bruising after being interrogated by police on his association with Israeli-Palestinian organisations

Israeli professors, students and rights activists are…

blocks.text: Israeli professors, students and rights activists are calling for the immediate release of Mahdi Tounsi, a sociology student at Jerusalem’s Hebrew University who has been held without charge for more than two weeks after he was seized from his dorm room.

The detention comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.
Police took Tounsi, 26, a criminology and sociology student from East Jerusalem who is active in Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, from his dorm room on 8 November.
When he appeared by video link at a court hearing on 19 November he had visible bruises on his face, did not have the glasses he needs to see properly, and his hair and beard had been shaved.

Tounsi told his lawyer that police beat him in the dorm, in the patrol car and at the police station, Israeli media reported. Interrogators questioned him about his activism with Israeli-Palestinian organisations Standing Together and Ir Amim.
Both groups called for his immediate release and warned against using security agencies to silence political activity and critical speech.

“[This] could happen to any student and any one of us, especially in a month when the government is persecuting Arab citizens, from [journalist] Abed Abu Shehadeh to the leaders of Arab political parties,” Standing Together said in a statement, calling on the university to intervene to ensure a fair judicial process.

Ir Amim described Tounsi as thoughtful, gentle and a valued partner “in movements bringing Palestinians and Israelis together”, in a statement that also warned of “serious concerns for his safety, wellbeing, and right to due process”.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators call for the release of Mahdi Tounsi outside the Jerusalem district court. Photograph: Jess Flom/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: After losing the election, Netanyahu and his allies weaponised false accusations of mass fraud – Israel’s election commission validated the results – in an attempt to hold on to power by delegitimising the votes of Palestinian citizens of Israel.
The prime minister has also been accused of politicising security institutions in his campaign against Palestinian-led parties, and fostering a rise in racist rhetoric.

When police powers to hold Tounsi under the original arrest warrant expired last week, they submitted an order to hold him without trial in administrative detention, signed by the defence minister, Israel Katz.

The administrative detention law allows Israel to hold individuals for up to six months without charging them or allowing them to see evidence against them, although it has to be presented in a closed court.
Because the Shin Bet security force did not send a representative to the hearing on Tounsi’s detention last week, it was postponed until Tuesday.

Ahead of the court hearing, Jewish and Palestinian students demonstrated at universities across the country, including Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, with signs including “Free Mahdi” and “Kidnapping Palestinians will not silence justice”.
The university authorities did not inform his family, and his detention only came to light after concerned friends reported him missing.

Hebrew University said in a statement that it was notified about the arrest shortly before police seized Tounsi, that no university representatives were present when he was detained and police afterwards said the arrest took place “without unusual incidents”.
It did not directly address the allegations of police violence, his visible bruising, the shaving of his head and beard, removal of his glasses or the shifting legal framework.

“The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings,” the statement said.
“We are concerned for his wellbeing,” the statement added, saying the university hoped “that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process”.
Israeli police did not respond to requests for comment about Tounsi’s detention.

Tounsi is a resident of East Jerusalem, not a Palestinian citizen of Israel. Palestinians holding that status can move freely inside Israel and Jerusalem but are stateless and can not vote in Israeli national elections.

articles.title: What happened at the Seattle airport? Outrage as ICE arrests man and daughter boarding flight
articles.summary: A chaotic scene unfolded at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport Saturday as a father and daughter were detained by masked immigration officers while boarding their flight bound for L.A.

blocks.text: World·New
A chaotic scene unfolded at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport Saturday as a father and daughter were detained by masked immigration officers while boarding their flight bound for L.A.
ICE says both had overstayed their visas
'They're taking my dad:' Masked ICE agents arrest passengers at Seattle airport
It's been described as "horrific," "chilling" and "distressing."

A chaotic scene unfolded at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday morning as a father and daughter were detained by masked immigration officers while boarding their flight at around 8 a.m. PST.

Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles recorded the struggle, which showed two men in unmarked jackets and khaki pants struggling with someone on the ground as onlookers screamed, cried and a woman shouted: "They're taking my dad."
The men "just lunged forward. They didn’t identify themselves and then sort of hit this family from behind," said passenger John Gaedeke, who filmed part of the confrontation.
The videos have since gone viral.
Lawmakers and other officials have decried the arrests, and protesters have been marching through the airport chanting "ICE out now."
A person argues with a police officer during a protest at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday. (David Ryder/Reuters)
So, what happened? Why did Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrest the father and daughter? And what happens to them now? Here what to know:
Who was arrested?

ICE officers conducted an operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, the agency said in a statement posted on social media, and also arrested, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, later identified as Mendoza's daughter.

A lawyer for them both says they were travelling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and have been seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015. They have no criminal record, said Olia Catala.

items: Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota released after federal court ruling
U.S. ICE agents shoot and wound man during arrest in New York City, sparking protests

blocks.text: "They’ve done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said.
Mejia "went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit," she said. "So it’s just heartbreaking."

Catala told local media that Mendoza brought his daughter to the U.S. when she was 14, and that they entered legally on tourist visas. Mendoza later filed an asylum claim, the attorney told NBC-affiliate King5 News, and Meija married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status.
"The entire family is traumatized," she told King5 News.

People react as ICE officers detain passenger on the jetbridge for an Alaska Airlines flight from Seattle to Los Angeles in this screengrab from a video obtained from social media and verified by Reuters. (John Gaedeke/Reuters)
Mejia’s husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were arrested, Catala said, but was not detained.
"This is a family whose lives have been turned upside down," Catala said Sunday in a statement posted to social media.
Both are being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said.
Why were they arrested?
The "targeted" operation was to arrest Mendoza, ICE said in a statement, describing him as "an illegal alien from Mexico" who had overstayed his visa.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said it no longer tolerates "aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country."
"This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport," DHS said in a statement to CBC News.

ICE said that, during the Saturday morning arrest, other travellers began to "obstruct and assault" the officers, and claims that one passenger "hurled hot coffee" at them. They identified her as Mejia, also calling her "an illegal alien from Mexico with visa overstay."

Video shared with @komonews shows part of the arrests made by masked ICE agents on a jet bridge at @flySEA this morning. The Port of Seattle said it was “outraged” by the incident and investigating. #seattle (Video: John Gaedeke) https://t.co/t6J6csdZ0R—clairecweber
ICE said Meija "will be charged with assaulting a federal officer."
Catala, their attorney, says Meija was holding a cup of coffee during the confrontation, but disputes that she threw it. Other passengers who witnessed the scene said it was knocked out of her hands.
"When somebody’s charging at you, you’re going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what’s going on."
People protest at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport Saturday. (David Ryder/Reuters)
What's the reaction?
In addition to the public backlash and protests, lawmakers and other officials have decried the arrests.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called the videos "horrific" and "chilling," and Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said she was "outraged" by the sight of masked ICE agents "causing chaos and dragging a woman off the jetway."
"ICE is completely and totally out of control and today we are confronted with yet more evidence of this," Ferguson told a news conference on Saturday.
"These tactics are unacceptable and un-American," Wilson said in a statement posted on social media.

items: Minnesota officials, Trump administration offer very different takes on ICE's detainment of boy, 5
Winnipeg-born Canadian released from U.S. immigration detention after 8 months in 'hellhole'

blocks.text: Washington Attorney-General Nick Brown also decried the arrests, writing on social media: "We are sick and tired of poorly trained masked federal agents vanishing people out of thin air.
"Washingtonians will never accept these stunts as legitimate or responsible law enforcement."
The Port of Seattle said in a statement it was "outraged" by the incident, adding that immigration enforcement at the airport are conducted without the port’s participation or knowledge.
"This incident was not only distressing for the affected family but the passengers around them, and Port officials continue to engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."
Alaska Airlines also said it wasn't provided advanced notice and that it was "concerned."
April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, called the ICE arrest a "smash-and-grab" action that injected fear and chaos during a delicate time for air travel.
The union includes local chapters representing flight attendants and ground crew at the airport.
A screengrab from a video obtained from social media, verified by Reuters, shows the scene on the jetbridge Saturday. (John Gaedeke/Reuters)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Tajikistan follows US call, withdraws from ICC
articles.summary: Tajikistan has initiated its withdrawal from the International Criminal Court as the US calls for it to be "dismantled." The decision was made during a recent visit from Russian President Vladimir…

image.caption: Tajikistan, a close ally of Russia, decided to leave the ICC during a visit from Russian President Vladimir PutinImage: Sergey Bobylev/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tajikistan has now become the fourth country to announce its formal withdrawal from the International Criminal Court (ICC) in the Hague, Netherlands since the US announced its intention to "dismantle" the body — joining Chad, Naoero [formerly Nauru] and Venezuela.

US President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have railed against the court as abusing its jurisdiction, with Trump publicly attacking the ICC during remarks at a trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin — who is wanted by the court for war crimes committed during the course of Russia's full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
Trump's public attacks on the world's permanent war crimes tribunal prompted an amused smirk from Putin during their meeting in Shenzhen, China.
Why is the ICC important?
The ICC prosecutes individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, crimes of aggression and war crimes in instances when national cannot or will not act.
The ICC issued an international arrest warrant for Putin in March 2023.
Tajikistan's government said it made the decision to initiate the one-year withdrawal process on Friday, when Putin made a stopover visit after leaving his trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi.
The ICC said it "regrets" Tajikistan's decision, adding that the move undermines "the collective pursuit of justice" and weakens "global efforts to end impunity."

"The ICC stands at the heart of the international system of accountability, and its effectiveness depends on sustained and unequivocal support from the international community," an ICC statement continued.
Tajikistan signed the Rome Statute that established the ICC back in 1998 and ratified it in 2000.
Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger have also announced their withdrawal from the court, blasting it as a tool of "neocolonial repression."

articles.title: Dentist pleads guilty to professional misconduct in 23-year-old's death
articles.summary: A Manitoba dentist charged under the provincial dental regulator's code of conduct in relation to the death of Virginia Blatz has pleaded guilty to professional misconduct.

image.caption: Virginia Blatz, 23, died on Nov. 27, 2024, after she went to have her wisdom teeth removed. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Breaking
A Manitoba dentist charged under the provincial dental regulator's code of conduct in relation to the death of Virginia Blatz has pleaded guilty to professional misconduct.
Virginia Blatz died after going to have her wisdom teeth removed
The dentist admitted during an inquiry hearing panel in Winnipeg on Monday morning that Blatz was given far more anesthetic than recommended.
Blatz, 23, was pronounced dead after she went to see the doctor to get her wisdom teeth removed on Nov. 27, 2024.

The dentist was charged with contravention of the Manitoba Dental Association's code of ethics, including going against the principles to do no harm, to improve the patient's condition and to provide competent care. He was also charged with professional misconduct.
He entered a guilty plea during Monday morning's hearing.
According to an agreed statement of facts, the dentist far exceeded the recommended dose of Articane — a local anesthetic drug typically given to manage pain — when providing care to Blatz.
The family of Virginia Blatz, 23, is suing the dentist. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

At time of her death, Virginia weighed about 100 pounds, and the dose given to her on the day of her death exceeded the maximum dosage that she should have been given by about 200 per cent, said an expert report included in the agreed statement of facts.
Her family is suing the dentist, his practice and the corporation that owns and operates the dental centre, alleging the care provided to Blatz was negligent.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Lauren Scott is a Winnipeg-based reporter with CBC Manitoba. They hold a master’s degree in computational and data journalism, and have previously worked for the Hamilton Spectator and The Canadian Press.

articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot ‘deeply shocked’ after nude images used to promote book
articles.summary:
French woman says she will pursue legal action against publisher and author over use of photos taken by convicted husband

Gisèle Pelicot has said she is “deeply shocked” that nude…

blocks.text: Gisèle Pelicot has said she is “deeply shocked” that nude photographs of her had been used without her consent to promote a psychoanalyst’s book that suggests she was complicit in her abuse.

Pelicot, 73, became a global icon in the fight against sexual violence in 2024 during the trial that saw her former husband convicted of drugging and raping her, as well as recruiting 49 other men to rape her while unconscious.

“I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes,” Pelicot told broadcaster BFM TV. “I refuse to let my privacy become an advertising tool.”

She said she would pursue legal action against Tinbad publishing house and the author, Sabine Prokhoris, who has described her book as “a critical examination of the notion of psychological control and domination”. One chapter concerns the Pelicot case.
Tinbad sent some media nude photographs and graphic videos of Pelicot that her husband had taken to promote the book, according to French weekly le Canard enchaîné.
“Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt,” Pelicot told the broadcaster. “As if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough.”
Tinbad has apologised, describing the episode as an “unfortunate communication error”.
The publisher maintained that it had not sent “any images of rape or any pornographic videos” to the press, while not denying that nude photographs had been distributed.
Prokhoris said she placed “full responsibility” for the “inappropriate” promotional campaign on her publisher.
According to her book’s back-cover blurb, it calls for readers to “think freely” about the notion of coercive control, described as “a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy”.
Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

articles.title: 'The land is ours': First Nation intends to mine sand in Manitoba through Sio Silica partnership
articles.summary: A Manitoba First Nation is planning to push ahead with a proposed sand mining operation to support a solar panel manufacturing facility, whether the provincial government likes it or not.

image.caption: Sheldon Kent, chief of Black River First Nation, would like the province to grant a licence for Sio Silica to harvest high purity quartz sand on First Nation land, but said the project will go ahead regardless. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A Manitoba First Nation is planning to push ahead with a proposed sand mining operation to support a solar panel manufacturing facility, whether the provincial government likes it or not.
'We have our own right to do it and we're going do this project,' says Black River Chief Sheldon Kent
Sheldon Kent, chief of Black River First Nation on the east shore of Lake Winnipeg, said his community is partnering with mining company Sio Silica to harvest high-purity quartz.
"We see the environmental plan [for the Sio Silica project] is sustainable, it's workable, it's safe," he said Monday at a news conference with the Southern Chiefs' Organization.
"We wouldn't get involved if it was going to be destructive and destroy what we have."
Kent said he's asking the province to work with Black River, but "we have our own jurisdiction, we have our own right to do it, and we're going to do this project" on First Nation land.

Specifically, he's talking about just over 1,000 hectares (2,500 acres) of land near near Vivian, about 50 kilometres east of Winnipeg. His community bought the land a few years ago because it saw economic potential, he said.
Kent expects sand harvesting to start as early as next year.

items: Sio Silica promises $125M sand-storage facility in Churchill, Man., if mining licence approved

blocks.text: The ideal scenario would be that Manitoba's NDP government grants a licence, Kent said, "but from a First Nations stand, the land is ours. We've always maintained and protected the land, [and] we are going to go forward with or without the province.
"I don't need to go to court. I'm just going to go occupy the land that we already have and we'll start mining it."
CBC News has reached out to the province for a response.
Southern Chiefs’ Organization Grand Chief Jerry Daniels is working toward acquiring up to 51 per cent ownership in a facility that would manufacture solar panels in Manitoba. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)
Kent spoke after Southern Chiefs' Grand Chief Jerry Daniels announced a preliminary agreement with German manufacturer RCT Solutions in a solar project that will rely on the sand.
The organization is working toward acquiring up to 51 per cent ownership in a facility that would manufacture solar panels and glass "here in Manitoba," said Daniels.
"An ownership stake could give our nations a say in how the facility is developed [and] operated, and share in the returns it will generate."
Those returns, particularly financial resources, could then be invested and used to support First Nations communities and their quality of life, he said.

"Opportunities like this can help a young person in one of our nations to learn a trade, build a career and raise a family close to home," said Daniels, adding First Nations businesses would also be able to bid on work to build, supply and operate the facility.

Peter Fath, CEO of the German manufacturer RCT Solutions, wants to build a solar panel production campus but says the company needs the high-quality sand that Sio Silica would mine. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

The head and founder of RCT Solutions, Peter Fath, said in July 2023 that he wanted to build a multibillion-dollar solar panel production campus near Winnipeg, which he said would employ close to 8,000 people.
"My solar sector is growing like hell, but we don't have enough high-purity quartz. You have the fuel of our industry," Fath said at Monday's news conference.
All four stages needed in the production chain of solar panels "are perfectly tagged by the quartz quality of Sio Silica," he added.
Sio Silica is hoping to obtain an environmental licence to drill for sand in the rural municipality of Springfield, but Premier Wab Kinew cast doubt in June on the prospect of Manitoba approving it.

items: Kinew casts doubt on approving Sio Silica's 2nd effort to obtain licence to mine sand

blocks.text: Kinew's NDP government denied an earlier Sio Silica application in 2024.
Fath said Manitoba, with its hydro and power, has a chance to become a green manufacturing hub of Canada with the addition of his company's solar panel manufacturing campus.
He was more conciliatory in his messaging to the province, saying without its support, "it will not work."
"I will not run against the wall and get a bloody head," Fath said.
The sand below the surface of southeastern Manitoba is 99.85 per cent pure silica. (Gary Solilak/CBC)
As for where the solar campus idea currently stands, he said it needs an engineering study and a feasibility study on a possible location. After that, an investment decision needs to be made.
Three potential sites have been identified but no location has been chosen, he said.
Fath said he's puzzled by the pushback to the Sio Silica project.

Everyone needs energy and wants it to be green, and Manitoba is sitting on "white gold," he said. The province has one of the world's largest deposits of quartz-rich silica, which could enable it to "build its own future," said Fath.
He repeated past claims it will be mined in a safe, sustainable way, and disputed concerns the process could contaminate drinking water.
"Let us work on fact-driven decisions," he said. "If I had any doubt on the negative environmental impact … I would not do the project, definitely not."
If anything did force a halt to mining, "I would lose hundreds of millions of dollars [of dollars] with my partners," said Fath.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.
With files from Josh Crabb

articles.title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
articles.summary: Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were reportedly given 74 lashes in Qom.

blocks.text: A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.
Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.
Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.
This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.
In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.
At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.
On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.
"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.
"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."
Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.
Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.
Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

articles.title: Comedian impersonates Trump's dance moves, mocks trade talks at Canada press dinner
articles.summary: The impersonator, Canadian comedian Mark Critch, poked fun at the US president's search for a new press secretary and US-Canada trade talks.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney brought a Donald Trump impersonator on stage at Ottawa's annual press gallery dinner, where he poked fun at strained US-Canada relations and on-again, off-again trade talks.
The impersonator, played by comedian Mark Critch of the sketch comedy show This Hour Has 22 Minutes, came out after Carney jokingly pressed an "emergency comedy button" during his speech.
Critch appeared alongside another actor impersonating Carney, played by Canadian sketch comedian Mark McKinney.
"We've got two Carneys here, it's a disaster," the Trump impersonator said after he walked on stage.

Using some of Trump's signature mannerisms, like his dance moves and his slightly hunched posture, he joked about the latest US midterm elections, which led to Trump's Republican Party losing control in Congress.
"I'm so popular we just had a big BLUE WAVE in the states," the impersonator said at the Saturday press gala.
He also took aim at ongoing US-Canada trade negotiations, saying,"We're going to have a great deal. There's only one thing standing in the way: me, because I'm crazy."
There were also jabs at Trump's search for a new White House press secretary following Katie Zacharia's exit, and at US ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra, who is unpopular among Canadians.
"I said 'find somebody who is less likeable than me,' and we got one," the Trump impersonator joked about Hoekstra.

Carney stood behind him occasionally laughing. The prime minister also delivered his own zingers, saying at one point: "This is a tough room. And I've been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator."

Both Critch and McKinney - the two impersonators - are fixtures of This Hour Has 22 Minutes, a long-standing Canadian sketch comedy show that has recently enjoyed viral internet fame for its timely skits mocking the Trump administration.
The skits, published directly on Tik Tok and YouTube, have depicted Zacharia's quick ouster, external and poked fun at rapper Nicki Minaj's, external support for Trump.
They have garnered millions of views, and even captured the attention of major US media., external

Critch and McKinney's appearance at Saturday's dinner is part of an evening of traditionally light-hearted humour, where Canadian politicians poke fun at one another at a gala hosted by the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery.
In a separate speech, Canada's governor general, Louise Arbour, joked about Carney's popularity and frequent global travel.

"Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he's supposed to be," Arbour said.

articles.title: 3 Calgary police officers charged with manslaughter in death of unarmed Blood Tribe man
articles.summary: Three Calgary police officers have been charged with manslaughter two years after an unarmed Blood Tribe man died while in police custody.

image.caption: Jon Wells, 42, died while in police custody in September 2024. On Monday, three Calgary police officers were charged with manslaughter. (Submitted)

blocks.text: Three Calgary police officers have been charged with manslaughter two years after an unarmed Blood Tribe man died while in police custody.

Jon Wells, 42, died in September 2024 after he was tackled, punched and subjected to other “uses of force” at the hands of officers, the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) said at the time.
"Jon was more than a headline, more than a statistic, and more than the circumstances of his death," wrote Wells' sister Leslie Wells in a statement on Monday.
"He was a son, father, brother and a friend and was deeply loved. He deserved to be protected, treated with compassion and given the opportunity to return home to those who loved him."

items: Unarmed man punched, tackled by officers in altercation that ended in his death: police watchdog

blocks.text: The incident took place in the lobby of the Carriage House Hotel and Conference Centre on Macleod Trail.
On Monday, three of the responding officers — constables Filip Poskovic, 39, Roy Braun, 53, and Vincent Washington, 48 — were charged with manslaughter and assault causing bodily harm.

In a statement released Monday, ASIRT said following its two-year investigation, which found "reasonable grounds to believe offences were committed," executive director Matthew Block — with support from the Alberta Crown Prosecution Service — made the decision to charge the three officers.
Leslie Wells said that while she views the charges as a step in the right direction, her faith in police has not been fully restored.

"Accountability is a step toward justice, but true justice must also lead to change. Indigenous families should not have to lose their loved ones for society to recognize the value of our lives. My brother’s life was precious long before his death brought attention to these injustices."
'Presumed innocent'
Defence lawyer Cory Wilson, who represents Poskovic, provided a brief statement to CBC News, saying his client denies the allegations.
“He is presumed innocent and plans to vigorously defend himself at trial,” said Wilson.
Shamsher Kothari, who represents Braun, also provided a written statement, saying his client “vehemently denies the charges laid today.”
“We look forward to his exoneration within the upcoming judicial proceedings,” Kothari wrote.
Defence lawyer Don MacLeod, who represents Washington, said his client "maintains his innocence and intends to mount a vigorous defence."
Handcuffs, spit hood
The officers were charged Monday morning at the ASIRT office and were released on an undertaking. They are due back in court in January.
All three are relieved with pay, according to the Calgary Police Service (CPS).

items: Hundreds march for Blood Tribe man who died in police custody

blocks.text: Wells died in the early morning hours of Sept. 17, 2024.
3 Calgary officers charged with manslaughter in death of unarmed Indigenous man

On that day, just before 1 a.m., police were called to the Carriage House Hotel after Wells allegedly refused to leave the lobby. On the day of the incident, CPS said in a release that Wells had been “acting erratically” and was “not co-operative.”
Officers used handcuffs, leg restraints and a spit hood on Wells who was face down on the ground. Minutes later, he was declared dead.
A spit hood — or spit mask — is a face covering that is draped over the heads of people who spit or threaten to as a protection for first responders.
Body-worn video footage
About a week after Wells’ death, ASIRT released details of the interaction between Wells and the officers on-scene based on body-worn camera footage.
According to ASIRT, Wells, who was unarmed, stood with his hands in full view when the first officer arrived and ordered him to leave.
The officer ordered Wells to leave the lobby. Wells acted “in a confused fashion,” according to ASIRT. He tried to pick up items off the floor “that were clearly non-existent.”
After about 30 seconds, the officer pointed his stun gun at Wells who put his hands up, asked the officer not to shoot and said he would leave.
'I don't want to die'
As Wells walked slowly to the main door with his hands raised he said to the officer, “I don’t want to die.” The officer ordered Wells to stop talking and continued to point his weapon at him.
Two other officers arrived through the main lobby door. Again, Wells stated that he didn’t want to die.
The first officer holstered his stun gun and tried to grab Wells.
“At no point during the interaction had the male been identified, nor was he ever told he was being detained or under arrest,” said ASIRT in its September 2024 statement.
'Various uses of force'
Wells “resists being grabbed” and was then tackled by a second officer who punched him in the head while both were on the ground.
The two other officers then shot Wells with their stun guns.
The three officers then spent the next three-and-a-half minutes administering “various uses of force” on Wells before restraining him with handcuffs and leg restraints.

items: Family of Blood Tribe man who died in Calgary Police custody calls for public inquiry

blocks.text: By then, Wells was vomiting and bleeding from the mouth. The officers put a spit hood on him as he laid face down on the floor.
EMS and other officers had arrived at this point and about seven minutes after he was handcuffed, paramedics administered a sedative to Wells, who was still face down.
Wells was left face down in handcuffs, leg restraints and the spit mask for another three minutes until someone at the scene noticed he was unresponsive.
Despite efforts by first responders, Wells was declared dead in the hotel lobby.
In a written statement, CPS called the charges “extremely serious,” and said it recognizes the “significant concerns” they raise regarding police accountability, the use of force and public trust.

“We understand that incidents like this can further challenge our relationships with all communities and reinforces the importance of transparency, accountability and meaningful engagement,” reads the statement issued Monday.
